#1077. Liverpool’s expensive attack feast on Palace to leave Sage looking doomed

Crystal Palace are playing this season as if afflicted by a curse. They seem to have made a terrible deal, possibly involving a monkey’s paw. As a result, Pierre Sage’s team were able to defend credibly for around 44 minutes of each half, on one condition: They must switch off completely, at least twice per game.

This being the Premier League, those lapses in concentration are usually punished. A mostly compact performance out of possession briefly became as porous as a bath sponge when Liverpool eased into a 2-0 lead, nine minutes after half-time. Florian Wirtz did not even need to finish cleanly to score his first Premier League goal of the season, striding on to an unopposed low cross from Bradley Barcola and killing the match as a contest.

Bradley Barcola and Florian Wirtz combine to put Liverpool 2-0 up! 🔴 https://t.co/F6sw33FkYZ

Major signings need to lay down a marker when arriving at Liverpool. Barcola has his hat-trick at LASK in the Champions League, but we are still waiting for a stirring big-match-defining contribution from him since his summer arrival. Arguably the same could be said for Wirtz, nearly 18 months since he joined.

Neither left Selhurst Park looking like the world-beaters they did occasionally for their previous clubs. Still, one misfiring attacker creating a goal for another represents progress and all great partnerships must start somewhere. Lennon and McCartney would improve after 1958’s Too Bad About Sorrows.

If there was ever a place for the least-productive expensively assembled attacking group in the league to find form it was surely south London on this Sunday lunchtime. Liverpool came in with two defeats in their previous two but, European trophy aside, it has been a lousy 2026 for Palace.

They have the most defeats of any ever-present Premier League team and began (and ended) the weekend with the worst defensive record. They have conceded twice as many goals from headers as any other team. Even their most loyal fan group has disbanded.

Alexis Mac Allister opened the scoring in gut-punching fashion, after a series of Palace near-misses. Chairman Steve Parish rubbed his face in the directors’ box, in the style of peak-stress era Guardiola. None of this looked good for Sage, who appears on the brink of dismissal, with Thomas Frank his most likely replacement.

Asked if he expected to remain in his job on the other side of the international break Sage said he deemed his prospects “better than you, I think”.

“We deserved better today,” the Frenchman said. “But football is not about what you deserve it is about how efficient you are and today we had a lack of efficiency”.

Counter-intuitively, it was Palace’s flashes of promise which suggested the Frenchman might be doomed. There is enough to work with here, and plenty going marginally against Palace to suggest a change in leadership might prompt a turnaround, however unfair it would be on their manager. Yéremy Pino hit the bar, Jorgen Strand Larsen had his composed close-range goal struck from the record by VAR, Daichi Kamada stung Alisson Becker’s palms and the Brazilian saved well again from Adam Wharton’s feathered header.

Jorgen Strand Larsen thought he had the opener against Liverpool, but it was ruled out for offside! ❌ https://t.co/JkSKbtkvak

The other factor which seems likely to condemn Sage is his team’s boneheaded defensive lapses. Liverpool were awarded a debatable free-kick out wide, Quinten Timber let Mac Allister run off him too easily and he duly nodded Dominik Szoboszlai’s delivery past Dean Henderson with ease. Another header conceded.

Liverpool have taken the lead against Crystal Palace thanks to Alexis Mac Alister's header! 💥 https://t.co/kNal7qsQ35

Mac Allister, formerly of Brighton, endeared himself to the Holmesdale Road Stand with a priggish celebration. There was some blowback from the seats closest, but a more dominant sense of resignation. Someone in the adjoining block took out their phone and snapped a picture. Formerly hated rival scoring against you, rubbing it in with his celebration: truly one to show the grandkids.

Liverpool had put together little of substance until then, with Wirtz drifting through another half, Alexander Isak looking keen but flawed and Barcola spooning a promising shot into low-Earth orbit. The second half was better, but Isak looked to have wasted his best chance, a one-on-one with Henderson thumped too close to the goalkeeper.

Isak had his moment in the end, checking back to finish calmly at the end of a counter-attack against a tiring defence. Eight for the season for him and an assist for Wirtz, too, although it was hardly a pass of Molbyesque majesty.

“Happy for him,” Iraola said of Wirtz, also praising Isak’s movement for the German’s goal. “I think [Wirtz] has been very unlucky in the Premier League, a couple of goals disallowed and situations where he deserves honestly to score.”

So it was Liverpool’s blip righted here, despite all of Palace’s pressure. Alisson, who took some flak for his performance at Fenerbahce, was hard to fault. He may not have reached Eddie Nketiah’s stoppage-time penalty, but made a series of brave saves and deserved a clean sheet. For all that attacking talent, the long-serving goalkeeper still looks like one of Iraola’s most important players.

13 - Liverpool have earned more points away from home in the Premier League this season than any other side (13). It's the Reds' joint-most ever from their first five away matches of a league campaign. Journeymen. https://t.co/lFe8MO3T6m

"We were efficient in front of goal" Florian Wirtz was happy with Liverpool's attacking display against Crystal Palace ⚽️ https://t.co/E0U2UJiiao

FULL TIME: Brighton's fine start to the season continues after a comfortable win against ten player Brentford, Florian Wirtz bags his first goal of the season as Liverpool inflict more pain on Crystal Palace, Bournemouth edge past Ipswich at Portman Road to continue their fine form and Sunderland pick up a huge win at home to Chelsea!

Liverpool condemn Palace to a fourth successive Premier League defeat. Mac Allister, Wirtz and Isak were all on target for the visitors, before Nketiah netted a last-gasp penalty. This result leaves Palace rooted to the bottom of the table following Sunderland’s win over Chelsea, while Liverpool move up to fourth. Will this end up being Sage’s last game in charge of Palace?

Finally, Alisson is beaten. Nketiah steps up and slams a confident penalty into the net. The Liverpool goalkeeper dives the correct way, but can’t keep it out as his clean sheet disappears. Palace’s attacking efforts have deserved a goal.

There’s a clash of heads in Liverpool’s penalty area as Kerkez and Osorio both challenge for the ball. The Hungarian catches the Palace attacker and he’s late, so the referee points to the spot.

Following that goal, Isak is withdrawn and replaced by Koumas. There’s four minutes of added time to end this game.

A good day but a middling performance from Liverpool. A goal for Wirtz, an assist for Barcola, and now Isak doing his bit for the revival narrative. Contributions from three of the most criticised members of Liverpool’s expensively-assembled attacking group. Not sure we will be seeing a great deal more of Pierre Sage in the Selhurst Park dugout.

Game, set and match for Liverpool. The visitors break as Munoz whips a cross into Wirtz, who has the composure to play in Isak. The striker cuts inside of a desperate challenge before smashing a clinical, close-range effort into the roof of the net. Palace fans flood out of Selhurst Park. Sage cuts a dejected figure on the sidelines.

"Isak's a Red, ole ole..." 🎶 https://t.co/ME0QB7Km48

Henderson makes a goal-saving stop. Mitchell fails to deal with a high clearance and Munoz pounces on the mistake before teeing up Isak. The Liverpool striker is through on goal, but Henderson does brilliantly to block his one-on-one effort. Sage makes a late double change as Khalaili and McNeil replace Mingueza and Pino.

Wirtz tests Henderson with a whipped attempt following Nyoni’s strong run and Munoz’s lay-off. However, the Palace captain makes a simple save.

Munoz tries to dribble away from Lerma, but the Liverpool substitute dives over the Palace man’s outstretched leg. Mac Allister then unnecessarily squares up to Lerma because of his annoyed reaction to Munoz’s simulation. As a result, all three of the aforementioned players are booked.

Palace can’t find a way past Alisson. Osorio drives down the wing and picks out the unmarked Pino, whose shot is smothered by the Liverpool goalkeeper. Lerma latches onto the loose ball, but Alisson is there once again to comfortably gather the Palace man’s ambitious rebound.

Liverpool continue to protect their two-goal advantage and make another forward change as Ngumoha comes on for Gakpo.

Sage makes an attacking change as Nketiah, who scored the winner against Liverpool at Selhurst Park in September 2025, replaces Strand Larsen up top.

In fairness to Palace, you can’t fault their effort. Liverpool are holding firm and the hosts are lacking end-product. Pino then catches Araujo with a late tackle to pick up a needless booking.

No need to be dramatic, but this does rather feel like the season for Pierre Sage. Losing games you have created the best chances in is a bad look for a manager under pressure, especially in the specific circumstances Palace are displaying. There is enough promise and talent in his team to suggest a different voice could extract more from the group. There is also a dreadful habit of switching off entirely, which might make a chairman wonder if it is time for more of a shouty presence in the dugout. The second Liverpool goal was woeful from a Palace point of view.

Iraola makes a double change as Nyoni and Munoz replace Szoboszlai and Barcola.

Alisson claims Wharton’s cross as Strand Larsen falls on the Liverpool goalkeeper. The Brazilian has been faultless today and looks well on the way to a deserved clean sheet as things stand.

The game has become quite chaotic and Palace’s shape has deserted them. If there’s another goal in this game, then it will be absolutely crucial. The hosts are waiting to craft a notable second-half chance.

Sage makes a change on the hour-mark as Osorio replaces Timber in the game’s first alteration.

Barcola is booked after halting a Palace counter with a forceful challenge through the back of Pino.

That second Liverpool goal has left Selhurst Park very deflated. All the noise is coming from the away fans. Mitchell’s makes a crucial intervention to block Barcola’s cross. Palace look so stretched now.

It’s an excellent team goal as two of Liverpool’s big-money attackers devastatingly combine. Barcola is released down the wing and finds Wirtz with a low, pinpoint cross. The German playmaker then sweeps a composed, first-time effort into the bottom corner, leaving Henderson rooted to the spot. It’s a wonderful finish and credit to Barcola for the assist. Palace are in trouble and have a mountain to climb.

Bradley Barcola and Florian Wirtz combine to put Liverpool 2-0 up! 🔴 https://t.co/F6sw33FkYZ

Palace have made a positive start to this second half. They win the ball high up the pitch and Kamada tees up Strand Larsen. The striker has a shooting chance, but his touch lets him down, allowing Jacquet to come across and make a tackle.

Timber slides a pass in behind Jacquet for Strand Larsen to chase. However, Alisson is alert to the danger and rushes off his line to collect possession.

We are back under way at Selhurst Park. Both sides are unchanged at the break. Can Palace find a way back into this contest?

A thoroughly entertaining first half at Selhurst Park comes to a close as Liverpool hold a slender 1-0 lead over Palace thanks to Mac Allister’s 40th-minute header. Palace struck the bar through Pino and had a Strand Larsen goal ruled out for offside, but Liverpool have also looked dangerous going forward and their opener came as no surprise to anyone. To Palace’s credit, they’ve really taken the game to Liverpool so far, forcing Alisson into a couple of notable saves. However, there was still boos at half-time and Sage has work to do.

Much fury and gnashing of teeth towards the referee Tony Harrington at half time. The tunnel entrance takes players and officials past some of Palace’s most vociferous fans and several were giving him their most strident opinions.

Anger mostly towards the free kick which led to the goal, but it didn’t seem too egregious a decision to me.

Score is very harsh on Palace, though with Kamada, Strand Larsen and Pino all coming desperately close. Exactly the sort of hard luck story you’d expect from a team in trouble.

We lead at the break 👊 #CRYLIV https://t.co/7e9WF0j1KA

Despite Szoboszlai’s enforced absence and Liverpool’s numerical disadvantage, Barcola leads an attack that creates a shooting opportunity for Wirtz, which is blocked by Disasi. From the resulting corner, Jacquet nods the ball into Araujo’s path, but he can’t quite sort his feet out and fluffs his lines from close range.

There will be three minutes of added time at end this first half. There’s a break in play as Szoboszlai is down and in need of treatment.

Alisson produces another sensational stop. A teasing cross is glanced towards goal by Wharton, whose header is parried away by the diving Liverpool goalkeeper. Alisson has been in inspired form so far this afternoon.

Palace almost instantly reply as Mac Allister blocks Timber’s effort, before Alisson tips away the Palace’s midfielder’s long-range shot.

The visitors have the lead. Szoboszlai whips in a free kick and Mac Allister escapes Timber at the near post, before glancing a brilliant header into the far bottom corner.

Liverpool have taken the lead against Crystal Palace thanks to Alexis Mac Alister's header! 💥 https://t.co/kNal7qsQ35

Alisson comes to Liverpool’s rescue as Kamada’s meets a cross with a volley, but the goalkeeper produces an incredible reaction to parry the ball away.

Barcola finds space at the back post and connects with Szoboszlai’s searching cross thanks to a smashed first-time volley under no pressure, but he hits it over. The winger has to get that on target. That’s a massive chance.

Palace score but the offside flag is up! Liverpool fail to clear a Palace corner as Mingueza finds Pino with a clipped cross. The Spaniard fires the ball across goal and Kamada diverts it into Strand Larsen’s path. From close range, the striker chips into the net and rushes to the corner flag to celebrate. However, his joy is cut short by the offside flag. VAR checks and confirms the onfield decision.

Szoboszlai swivels and tries to find Wirtz with an intricate pass. The German playmaker made a darting run into the penalty area, but Wharton was there to make a pivotal sliding interception.

Jacquet rises highest within a sea of bodies to meet Szoboszlai’s corner, but he loops a header over the bar.

Araujo takes a loose touch and lunges into a late challenge on Mitchell, catching the Englishman on the ankle. The Palace bench jump up and the home players rush to the referee, who pulls out a yellow card. Araujo’s tackle was reckless and dangerous. It’s right on the verge of a red, but he escapes that punishment. The Liverpool defender needs to be careful now.

Palace strike the bar! The hosts make a rare foray forward as Mitchell finds Pino with a pinpoint cross. The Spaniard weaves into some space between two Liverpool defenders and slams a powerful half-volley against the woodwork.

Szoboszlai hangs a deep cross towards the back post. Gakpo directs it back across goal with a first-time volley, but no Liverpool has the attacking instinct to take a chance and anticipate it. Isak was instead loitering near the penalty spot. The visitors are well on top here.

Palace have been careless in possession so far, prompting groans from the home support. Szoboszlai draws a save from Henderson with a bobbling long-range strike, forcing the Palace captain into conceding a corner.

Liverpool are popping the ball around with real intent as Gakpo clips a teasing cross into Barcola. It’s just out of the winger’s reach, with Barcola claiming he was pushed by Mingueza. After seeing the replays, the Palace man just eased the Frenchman off the ball. There was minimal contact. Liverpool then win a free kick after Mingueza blocks Kerkez’s run, but Mac Allister glances Szoboszlai’s cross into the side netting at the near post.

Fun start. Palace have occasionally looked like they are hanging on for dear life when defending, especially whenever Gakpo has been on the ball, but have looked capable of some attacking threat of their own, through Pino and Timber especially. Barcola the first example of a player obeying Iraola’s advice to go down more, collapsing from a gentle push after climbing for a header he was never like to reach. Gets short shrift from the referee and Palace fans.

It’s been a fast-paced and frantic start to this game. Isak’s delightful touch takes him away from Disasi, who pulls the Liverpool forward to the ground, giving the visitors a free kick. The Palace defender is perhaps lucky to avoid a yellow card for that foul.

Mitchell lashes a dangerous delivery across the six-yard box towards Strand Larsen, but solid defensive work from Van Dijk and Araujo allow Liverpool to clear.

Barcola lofts a ball over the top of Palace’s backline for Isak to latch onto. However, Disasi recovers well and blocks the Liverpool striker’s fierce half-volley from a tight angle.

A loose pass at the back from Palace gifts Liverpool an early opportunity, but Henderson does well to get down low and gather Mac Allister’s low, fizzing effort from outside the penalty area.

Liverpool get us under way at Selhurst Park. Can Iraola inflict more misery on Sage?

This is my second visit to Selhurst since the Holmesdale Fanatics ultras group decided to hang up their large drum and all-black outfits. The atmosphere is noticeably less fierce. A pretty meek rendition of Glad All Over greets the players as they come out of the tunnel, althoiugh it is hardly the sort of rabble-rousing song to strike fear into an opponent at the best of times. Now you will experience the full power of the Dave Clark Five.

The whole of Selhurst Park observes a minute’s silence to remember those who lost their lives in war.

The Palace and Liverpool players are out on the pitch. Both sides are looking to return to winning ways in the Premier League before the international break.

More of an old school approach for Palace, some shots at a keeper pretending to dive properly and that classic English football activity - standing as far as you can from one another and hoofing the ball back and forth.

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of this Premier League match between Crystal Palace and Liverpool at Selhurst Park.

The pressure is building on Palace head coach Pierre Sage, who desperately needs a win to lift the mood and propel the club out of the relegation zone. Nottingham Forest’s impressive 3-1 win over Manchester City on Saturday evening means that Palace have dropped to a lowly 19th and are two points from safety. To make matters worse, Sage’s beleaguered side have also conceded the most goals in the division (21 in nine games).

On Thursday night, Daichi Kamada’s stoppage-time equaliser rescued a 1-1 home draw in the Europa League against Hoffenheim, after Palace delivered an alarmingly lacklustre performance.

Meanwhile, Liverpool also endured midweek European torment, as Andoni Iraola’s men fell to an error-ridden 3-2 defeat away at Fenerbahce in the Champions League, having previously lost 1-0 to Arsenal in their most recent Premier League encounter on Merseyside last weekend, which has left the club in sixth but just five points behind second-place Man City.

Speaking to reporters on Friday, Iraola said: “I think that’s the challenge, especially in a club like Liverpool. One week ago in this same press conference, we were on a run, everything was in a good place and we were in a better mood. And now, two defeats, it changes. It has to change and it has to be like this in a club like ours. Now we have to react after two defeats.”

As for Palace’s team news, Jean-Philippe Mateta is serving the first match of a three-game domestic ban after he was sent off for Palace in the 2-0 defeat to Tottenham last time out in the league. Liverpool’s long-term absentees include Hugo Ekitike, Giovanni Leoni, Conor Bradley and Jeremie Frimpong, while Ryan Gravenberch could also miss out after struggling with a heel injury.

Kick-off is at 14:00, with team news arriving shortly.

#1071. Super subs, xG kings and $150 million question marks: The Premier League's most intriguing players

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Whatever you might think about the November international break, there is one fact you simply will not be bothered to argue against: it is well timed for the statistically-minded football fan in your life. A 10-game sample size -- that's the useful stuff. At this point, many but not all teams are what their analytics tell us they are. It's similar but not quite the same for players. Not many have hit the 900-minute mark yet but plenty are at 500-plus, a body of evidence that usually isn't warped by any one good or bad game. Of course, it depends on how good or bad that game is.

We are not yet, then, at the stage where we can always draw hard and fast conclusions. We are, however, in a position to find some interesting questions. Here are five of them, in player form:

Spend $100 million on a player who turns 29 next week and the expectation is surely that a player will hit the ground running. That's especially true when they're Bruno Guimaraes, terror of Premier League midfields in a Newcastle United shirt, a player who had long since seemed ready to step up to a Champions League contender. While it would be fair to say that the Brazilian's form is nothing like a problem for table-topping Arsenal, he has not exactly started like a house on fire. Mikel Arteta has acknowledged as much whenever he has spoken about Guimaraes, even when served up the opportunity to praise him after what seemed an impressive performance against Hull City.

"He's hitting serious levels now, but we can still take him to another level. That's my conviction; I told him that in the dressing room -- he owned a lot of moments in the game, but there is still much more to come." It would be fair to say that, Hull aside, the best levels he has hit have been as a substitute. When he comes off the bench, he passes more accurately, wins more tackles, creates chances and scores brilliant goals. As a starter, he has occasionally looked a beat off his teammates.

Physical data from Gradient Sports hints as to what the issue might be. For every 90 Premier League minutes on the field, Guimaraes covers less of it at sprint speed (≥25 km/h) than any outfield player bar Mikel Merino and spends notably more time jogging than anyone, an average of 30 minutes. Compare Guimaraes to Declan Rice, an admittedly vertiginous bar, and it is easy to see why the new guy looks off the pace.

Equally, it explains why he's such a compelling substitute. When the other 21 players on the pitch are flagging, Guimaraes' comparative physical issues go unexposed and he can run the show.

That's all well and good for now but he can't carry on like this, can he? You would have to assume that Myles Lewis-Skelly will have to make way even if the academy graduate's emergence as a midfield option unlocked an improved Declan Rice at the tail end of last season. The second most expensive signing in your history can't be an impact guy off the bench behind the homegrown kid, right? Probably not but if there's any team that could justify the idea of Guimaraes as a 12th man, maybe it's Arsenal, where they pride themselves on their game-changing finishers.

Erling Haaland's Swiftian reign at the top of the Premier League xG chart has been interrupted, at least temporarily, by an unlikely source. You'd have to go back to the days of a marauding Romelu Lukaku for the last time an Everton striker looked like they might rule the roost. Only once since the Belgian's departure has an Evertonian cleared 20 goals in all competitions. In the last five even a dozen has been beyond this club.

Thierno Barry isn't there yet but boy is he on the right trajectory. His 7.28 non-penalty expected goals (npxG) puts him 0.22 ahead of Haaland and nearly 2.5 npxG up on anyone else in the league. Expand the pool to Europe's top five leagues and he is breathing rarefied air behind the top four of Lamine Yamal, Donyell Malen, Raphinha and Kylian Mbappe, all of whom have the advantage that they are not playing for an upper midtable outfit in the continent's most competitive division. And in that environment, Barry is making the hardest thing in the sport look easy: getting good shots in prime locations.

If Barry were turning them in as often as he was getting them, Everton might be even higher than sixth. Still, six goals through 10 games is not to be sniffed at, particularly when the pressure on the 24-year-old was so intense. The bungling of a deadline-day move for Folarin Balogun as Beto moved to Fiorentina meant that it was Barry or bust for David Moyes this season.

Perhaps it was an enforced show of faith for a player who was in and out of the XI last season, his first in England, that brought the best out of the former Villarreal man. His manager views the success in more straightforward terms. "He has settled down a bit more," said Moyes after Barry's brace helped down Coventry. "His language, his understanding, his communication is much better and he has worked hard to get himself in those positions to score."

It is easy to see why getting the soft factors right might have been all that was required. Barry is the ideal striker for the modern Premier League. Tall, strong and mobile -- he ranks third among center forwards for top speed this season, per Gradient Sports -- he can serve as an outball when a press needs beating and then get in the box. He might not have the technical elegance of an Mbappe but he makes his presence felt and occupies high-value spaces. That is more valuable than it sounds, as proven when James Tarkowski's howitzer from range deflected in off him. You might not like it but this is what elite center forward play looks like. Long may it continue, at least as far as Everton are concerned.

There are three types of underrated footballers. First, your common-or-garden-variety underrated footballers, often to be found plying their trade at Wolverhampton Wanderers or Burnley. The Ashley Westwood in that season he put up stupidly high xA numbers. Then there are the so often dubbed underrated that they actually become a bit overrated. Leighton Baines. Lee Carsley. They don't have to play for Everton but it does help. Olivier Giroud is another. See, not all Everton.

The most rarely spotted of the underrated is the chameleonic one, correctly pegged for a while only to develop such that he is underrated in a completely different way to how he once was. Take Alex Iwobi. Some time ago, a consensus coalesced around the Nigeria international that he was a good player for a team at Fulham's level (and indeed Everton's). Any minute when he was on the field, he would probably be delivering good performances for good Premier League teams.

Not anymore. Ten games in and Iwobi looks like one of the outstanding creative forces in the Premier League, critical to the march towards adequacy that Fulham have undertaken after a slow start to life with Alvaro Arbeloa.

Among true playmakers, Iwobi is one of the best at getting the ball into dangerous areas and creating for his teammates. Iwobi leads the league in expected assists with 2.95 and is tied with Bruno Fernandes for most passes completed into the penalty area. Only Pascal Gross has created more chances.

Those players can't match Iwobi when it comes to ball progression either. In terms of advancing the ball not just into the box but from deeper, Fulham's ball-playing fulcrum on the inside left channel has completed more progressive passes than anyone not named Declan Rice or Jan Paul van Hecke.

When Iwobi broke through at Arsenal, he displayed a preternatural sense for how to keep attacks alive, the pass before the pass before the pass. Now a 30-year-old, Iwobi still does that more than he unpicks defenses. One cannot argue, however, that he is not putting his teammates in the right spot. It is just that not everyone quite appreciates how often he does so just yet, including his own supporters, who jeered Iwobi when he was substituted in the early-season defeat to Crystal Palace. Since then, he has responded to his critics in style, teeing up two or more shots in each of Fulham's last seven Premier League matches. If a few more of them had been converted, in fact, if any of them had been converted, then Iwobi might not still be underrated.

The upper reaches of the list of most expensive transfers of all time are hardly all bangers all the time but of the biggest money moves in the sport's history there are only a handful where at such an early stage you find yourself wondering if anyone really understood what the plan was. Manchester City committed the best part of $150 million on Enzo Fernandez this summer, a fee only eclipsed by Neymar and Kylian Mbappe. Beyond a vague sense that it would be nice to give new manager Enzo Maresca one of his favorite players, what was it they had in mind?

We pointed out earlier in the season that the aggressive positioning of Fernandez in the 5-3 win over Sunderland looked extreme; at the time it seemed reasonable to view it as a reflection of a stretched-out, chaotic game. Maresca had, of course, unlocked more number 10-ish qualities in the Argentine at Chelsea but surely that had been reflective of what that team needed, particularly as Cole Palmer went off the boil? Perhaps not. Fernandez keeps popping up in the sort of positions that leave Elliot Anderson on an island. It is one thing to view Anderson as the new Rodri, quite another to immediately throw the England international in at the deep end, tying a whole midfield together by force of will.

Of course you could sketch out a logic for why you might push Fernandez high. It is not so long ago that City deployed two playmakers in front of a sitting midfielder and they ruled the Premier League. Fernandez and Rayan Cherki aren't Kevin De Bruyne and David Silva though.

Maybe Cherki could be offering a level of creation on a par with City greats; he started well enough last season. In year two, he is creating lower-quality chances, his expected assists per 90 dropping by 50%, notably more than the slight uptick in the quality and quantity of shots he is taking. It's no surprise that Cherki is creating less when fewer of his touches are coming in the attacking third. The output has been there so far, five goals and two assists in nine Premier League games, but for that to continue, Maresca might want to be getting his No. 10 into more dangerous spots.

Instead, those seem to be going to Fernandez, who has not proven himself able to get the final-third production to justify his platforming. For every 100 touches he takes, he is delivering significantly less npxG+xA than in either of the previous two seasons. Meanwhile, he less effective without the ball than he has been at any stage since coming to England. That's no wonder. If an opponent passes through City's frontline, then Fernandez does not have the mobility to get back.

As such, to enable themselves to get perhaps a shot or two more than they would get with Ayyoub Bouaddi or Mateo Kovacic next to Anderson, City have made themselves an even more vulnerable side to the counter attack, already giving up more fast-break openings than they did in 2020-21 or 2021-22. Carry on like this, and Fernandez will become one of those nine-figure transfers, the ones that live in infamy.

It was a signing that delighted a city when it was announced in early August, and rightly so. Loaning Carl Rushworth from Brighton had been an inspired bit of business by Coventry City, the then-24-year-old goalkeeper anchoring the best defense in the division as Frank Lampard's side returned to the top flight for the first time in over a quarter of a century. A club-record £22 million fee seemed a snip for such a young talent.

All of that is worth bearing in mind given the struggles Rushworth has endured this season: saving just 53.7% of shots he has faced, conceding 5.19 more goals than the xG value of the shots he has faced. The swagger of last season has been replaced by a sloppiness apparent in both the goals he conceded in the second half against Tottenham, weak gloves doing nothing to repel efforts that came at him a bit quicker and a bit sooner than they might have last year.

None of this needs to be a problem for Rushworth. In 2023-24, James Trafford was another highly touted young goalkeeper afforded a shot at the big time by Burnley. He was obliterated up and down the Premier League, his first touch in the division picking the ball out of the net off Erling Haaland. Those struggles were the making of him as they have broken others. It'll be some time yet before we discover which way these past few months send Rushworth.

#1069. Kansas City Current's grit earns them spot in NWSL Championship while Gotham's logisitcs problems linger

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

NEW YORK – The awkward logistics of Sunday's NWSL semifinal at Icahn Stadium, a quirky little venue sandwiched on an island in between Manhattan and Queens, were supposed to give way once Gotham FC and the Kansas City Current took to the pitch for one of the league's showpiece matches. When the Current's Croix Bethune opened the scoring in the 20th minute with an incredible looping shot off a free kick, the theme of the day was in motion. The league would make the best of the unideal circumstances with a top-quality soccer game, or at least with a few highlight-reel moments nestled into a match contested by a collection of the world's most talented players.

"I've been working on free kicks all year," Bethune said post-match, the Current justified in their decision to sign her last winter even if the validation was no longer needed, "and a lot more leading into the playoffs so just practice makes perfect."

Icahn Stadium's irregularities, though, seemed to reflect the game it unexpectedly became the host of six days earlier. The Current's 2-1 win came courtesy of a chippy game plan that would have been the case if the match had taken place at a traditional soccer-specific stadium but it felt especially at home at Icahn Stadium and amidst its elements. The teams played against the wind during New York's first properly cold weekend of the season, and Gotham faced a setting sun that impacted their vision during the first half. Bethune's impressive strike was really the only on-field spectacle to be witnessed on Randall's Island.

BEND IT LIKE BETHUNE 💫 KC takes the lead!NWSL Playoffs presented by Google Pixel pic.twitter.com/F4mQePT5QJ

"We knew it was going to be a physical game, without a doubt," Current forward Haley Hopkins said. "Like I said a million times, Gotham's a very, very good team and so we had to be super disciplined in our structure and catch them on their transition and we were just able to put the ball in the back of the net when we had our opportunities."

The introduction of Gotham's Rose Lavelle, who has been dealing with niggling fitness issues over the last few weeks, did not change the smash-and-grab energy of the game. Much as there was a week ago in their quarterfinal win over the Seattle Reign, there was a dull quality to Gotham's attack despite their star power. Over 180 minutes of possession play, the NWSL Shield winners managed zero shots on target and 0.66 expected goals, their midseason marquee signing Sam Kerr managing no shots along the way and mustering just one attempt in her last five matches. To say they were unlucky would be a stretch but their lively start to the second half gave their failed attempts to put a shot on frame a comedic feel.

"I think we were kind of our own worst enemy today," midfielder Savannah McCaskill said. "I think at times we played into what they wanted to do and their style of play. They want a very chippy game. They want to get into tackles. They want to draw fouls. They want to break up the game. They want to play long and that's not our style. We want to keep the ball. We want to control tempo, and we like to play pretty football. That's [what] we pride ourselves on … but I think we need to find a better way to balance that out, especially in this league. How can we meet the demand of a chippy game while also controlling the tempo? I think we did a really good job when we played them at home the last time [a 2-1 win on Aug. 14]. They scored early but then we completely dominated the rest of the game and I think we failed to do that today and so I think that's really the determining factor."

In other words, it was the perfect setup for Gotham to equalize off an own goal from Laney Rouse, a week after benefiting from another own goal from the Reign's Jordyn Bugg. Those two goals would be the only ones in their postseason run, just as one might expect from the NWSL Shield winners and reigning champions who entered the playoffs as the favorites to win another title.

Gotham FC find a way to tie up the semifinal 💪NWSL Playoffs presented by Google Pixel pic.twitter.com/Itbzs4Bhz1

Gotham goalkeeper Ann-Katrin Berger then slipped into game-saving mode with two important blocks while defender Tierna Davidson did what she could to hold the Current at bay, attempting to create a villain arc rivaled only by Argentina's run to the World Cup final. Though the hosts had lucked their way into an even game by the 88th minute, the dark and cold conditions at a downsized stadium in an obscure part of New York meant the game beckoned for extra time. One final smash and grab was undoubtedly in the cards, though where it would come from was hard to guess – the Current had put in the work to win but soccer's chaotic nature had already weaseled its way into the game.

In the end, it was the Current's Haley Hopkins who had the final say in the 89th minute off of – what else – a set piece, a free kick that led the forward to finally evade Berger with a shot off the crossbar. After losing to them twice in three previous meetings this season, the Current earned their spot in next week's NWSL Championship (Saturday, 8 p.m. ET, CBS, Paramount+) on the back of a well-executed gameplan.

HALEY HOPKINS CLUTCH OFF THE CROSSBAR 🤯The KC Current lead 2-1!NWSL Playoffs presented by Google Pixel pic.twitter.com/BT2OZhwX1y

"As much as we tried to analyze certain teams in the league that have given them trouble, we really took information from the games we've played against them, all the ways they challenged us," Current head coach Chris Armas said. "There's been games even where they get high [expected goals], too much progression, too much in our box and we just tried to then look at all the scenes and moments when we made it hard for them so we just tried to take from yesterday and apply it to today, [that] type of thing. We gave up zero shots on goal in 90 minutes. The commitment from our players to just will themselves to it to stick to a match plan that was going to be largely about taking away spaces, controlling the middle of the pitch and if we can do that on the day – and and we did that by running after them, too, and pressing in moments of high intensity – we not only might stop what they're trying to do on one end and maybe force the turnovers that could challenge them so a little bit of a chess match there in moments."

The Current were no slouches, finishing fourth in the regular season and now on a  seven-game winning streak en route to next week's championship. Bethune's star quality shone on Sunday, while the team's record with two-time NWSL MVP Temwa Chawinga and U.S. women's national team standout Michelle Cooper is formidable. It did not erase the fact that they slayed a giant along the way, knocking out the Shield winners and a team that had picked up five major titles in four seasons.

"Gotham has just raised the bar around the league and in our country here, so the way they play, the way the coach sets them up, the talent on the team, the type of games they can put you in, you have to come with a plan," Armas said. "They're a team that, again, if iron sharpens iron type of thing, we try to push teams and we try to raise the bar."

Gotham, though, had not looked the part of the NWSL's gold standard team. Their drastic run, while currently headlined by USWNT players Lavelle and Jaedyn Shaw, is built on the back of an effective defensive structure that has carried an inconsistent offense. Lavelle and, in particular, Shaw have picked up much of the slack en route to the NWSL Shield and Kerr was supposed to bolster their attack after Esther Gonzalez's shock departure for Saudi club Al Qadsiah. They finished the regular season sixth in the NWSL for expected goals with 49.01 but had a genuine finishing problem, notching just 39 goals and ranking in the league's bottom six in that category. Head coach Juan Carlos Amoros is not sounding the alarm just yet but as they enter another offseason, the attacking composition of the team deserves yet another look.

"Of course, we want to create more chances, more shots," Amoros said. "We all do but we look at the way we play. We look at the way we create chances. We look at who does that. I think when it comes to these games, could we have [made] some better decisions? Yes, we did. We actually create some good moments. Yes, I wouldn't over-think about it. Something that I'm happy [about]? No but at the same time, we work a lot to make sure that those moments happen. So you know the set pieces, those situations, the open plays, final decisions … Definitely, something that we want to be better [at]. We want to score more goals. I think that we are the best team defending in the league with our aggressive approach to defending but we want to also be able to create and score more goals."

More importantly, though, Gotham were not treated like the bar-raising team they have become over the years. Icahn Stadium has its charms and is a worthy inclusion on the list of wacky and wonderful places that embody American soccer, an enjoyably chaotic slice of the world's most popular game. It was also a back-up plan for a team that has called Sports Illustrated Stadium home for five years, settling in nicely to a state-of-the-art soccer-specific build for MLS' Red Bull New York that can hold 20,000 more fans than the 5,000-seater Icahn Stadium can. The pitch at Sports Illustrated Stadium, managed by RBNY, had fallen into disrepair and with the primary tenants' end-of-season friendly scheduled for the night before, there was not enough time to fix it. The quirks of Icahn Stadium only served as a reminder that Gotham – and the NWSL – should not have actually been there, even if the field at Randall's Island was better suited for the occasion.

"I want to be really clear and direct in saying that in these types of situations, the field is never an excuse," winger Midge Purce said. "We lost today because we weren't the better team. That being said, I would say it's inexcusable. It's not what you want in a professional league. It's not what you want for women who are progressing in the United States and supposed to be one of the best leagues in the entire world. I think it's a bad look for everyone involved and we always want to be at Sports Illustrated [Stadium] in front of our fans when we earned that right throughout the season but I would say it had no effect on performance today."

The Current's trip to Icahn Stadium is not where the NWSL's efforts to make lemonade end, either. Saturday's semifinal, in which the Washington Spirit beat the Utah Royals to book their spot in a championship game at their home of Audi Field, only added to it. One of the Spirit's sponsors underwrote the costs to push the start time of the Secretaries' Cup, a Division III football game, by a few hours but both matches were played on a field with soccer and football lines. The football lines will likely be faint but visible for next week's NWSL Championship, while the playability of the actual field will probably face a few questions in the build-up.

"I think we will never know what happened if we would have played [at Sports Illustrated Stadium] on a good pitch," Amoros said. "I think it was the right decision to come here. I think the pitch in the other stadium was unfortunately unplayable under our view. The last couple of games we picked up injuries. Luckily, nothing that has been a season-ending injury but we have to protect our players and guarantee the quality of football so to thank the club, obviously.

"Overall, I think it's been a sad weekend. I think also the situation in Washington yesterday. This league deserves better. The two, arguably, best teams, [most] consistent, having to deal with these situations and then yesterday, you sit down to watch that game around the world and you're seeing those American football lines across today. Credit to the club and the fans. I think they've done an amazing job here. The fans welcomed us. The club has really shifted everything to play here but we couldn't play in our ground where we could have had more people, where we are unbeaten in 13 games at the moment and but I think we took that decision, putting players' safety first, and the outcome is the outcome."

#1068. Non-league club’s first match since player’s death abandoned due to serious injury

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Defender Ethan Creary suffered a double break to his collarbone seven minutes into Hendon FC’s match on Saturday

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

A non-league club’s first match since a player’s death was called off due to a serious injury to another player.

Hendon FC were slated to play Bedfont Sports in the Isthmian League South Central Division this Saturday, in their first game since midfielder Ezekiel Williams died in hospital on 2 November.

Players from both clubs observed a minute’s silence to pay their respects before the match.

However, it was called off seven minutes in after an injury to defender Ethan Creary, who was taken off the pitch on a stretcher and to hospital.

The club announced hours later that Creary was “conscious, talking, and feeling better than earlier”.

“Early signs are that he's suffered a double break to the collarbone, possible shoulder ligament damage and concussion,” the club explained.

A further update on Sunday, posted on the club’s X account, featured a message from Creary: “I have a double break to the collar bone, will find out sometime this week whether it requires surgery. I have to be in the ward for 24hrs to assess any potential bleed in the brain, it’s just protocol and I woke up feeling okay.

“The reason I wanted to come here boys is because something special will happen here. Nothing changes in my eyes, with God & Ezekiel watching over us, no one can stand in our way.”

A statement by Hendon on Sunday said that a new date for the postponed game against Bedfont Sports would be announced “in due course”.

26-year-old Williams died due to head injuries suffered in an incident in Milton Keynes in the early hours of 1 November. Two men have since been charged with murder.

#1067. Chelsea bullied by Brian Brobbey and Sunderland

Talk about cramming everything in. Brian Brobbey only played for 67 minutes but, in that time, he collected a yellow card, ripped Levi Colwill’s shirt and earned himself a standing ovation after morphing into a battering ram.

Régis Le Bris, Sunderland’s head coach, said there was nobody like the Netherlands striker in the Premier League and it said everything that everyone wanted to make Brobbey centre of attention after a long overdue home win, even though he had not scored. Everyone, that is, bar Xabi Alonso.

“No, he’s not unstoppable,” Chelsea’s head coach replied when asked why his team had found Brobbey too much to handle. “He’s stoppable – but only when you defend better than we did. We were not bullied. We didn’t produce enough.”

That is one way of putting it. Another would be to say Brobbey was everything that Chelsea, much to Alonso’s disgust, were not: a bristling menace, a steamroller wearing a pair of boots, a player on a mission to help transform the mood – Enzo Le Fée’s decisive spot kick owed everything to Brobbey.

Chelsea arrived on Wearside looking to establish themselves in the top four ahead of the break but, instead, Alonso watched through his fingers as Sunderland reminded everyone why they were the joyous story of last season, a beautiful mix of inspiration and perspiration.

In fairness to the Chelsea manager, he refused to get caught in the minutiae of contentious penalty decisions – one that Chelsea were denied, another that they conceded – and could only lament as Sunderland ground out their first Premier League win since August 30, 70 long days ago.

“It wasn’t the best game,” Alonso said. “I think that we didn’t deserve more than probably one point, maybe. We need to be more consistent on the move, to get the ball from one side to the other, and we didn’t do that good enough. We didn’t produce enough to deserve to win.”

Unlike Sunderland. If you had turned up at the Stadium of Light without looking at the Premier League table, you would not have believed the hosts were bottom and you would not have given credence to the idea Le Bris, who has worked miracles these past two years, was under pressure.

Things, however, could not have started worse for Le Bris. Though Granit Xhaka has not shown last season’s form in these challenging opening months, the game plan was built around him, so to see the Sunderland captain hobbling off after three minutes was symptomatic of how things have gone for the Wearsiders.

“He felt something in the final sprint of the warm-up,” Le Bris explained. “We don’t know how bad it is.”

He is not the kind of coach, though, who will bemoan bad fortune. Le Bris sent on Jules Ahoka to replace Xhaka and watched as he, along with colleagues in red and white, set about trampling all over Chelsea’s intentions with incessant hard work.

Yet there was more to it. Sunderland can play, either intricately or directly, and a lovely move in the 12th minute needed a desperate, sliding intervention from Pep Chavarría’s to stop Trai Hume’s volley sliding in at the far post.

In the next attack, another Chemsdine Talbi cross – the Moroccan having been found by a peach of a pass from goalkeeper Robin Roefs – invited Brobbey to inflict maximum damage, but the Dutchman made a hash of his opportunity.

So close for Brobbey! 🤏 Sunderland almost take the lead against Chelsea. https://t.co/CUE6jHbPH2

The momentum could have changed completely in the 23rd minute. Alonso, his players and staff were convinced they would be given a penalty after Cole Palmer tumbled when his legs tangled with Luke O’Nien but, after a lengthy delay, VAR Nick Hopton felt there was no case to answer.

Hopton was involved again in the 33rd minute but, as Alonso said, Chelsea only had themselves to blame. Colwill simply could not contain Brobbey when he began marauding, grappling, grabbing and clipping the Dutchman’s heels. Le Fée did the rest, sending Mike Penders the wrong way.

Enzo Le Fee dispatches the penalty as Sunderland take the lead against Chelsea! 🔴⚪️ https://t.co/cCtYsHVWB9

From that point, Chelsea were in trouble, no matter how many changes Alonso made. They huffed, puffed, but nothing worked. They had come up against a red-and-white wall, fortified by constant backing from the stands, and the west Londoners were never going to knock it down.

One incident, as the clock ticked towards 90 minutes, encapsulated everything good about this Sunderland display when O’Nien chased down substitute Geovany Quenda to make a challenge. Another moment of defending from Thomas Meunier on Morgan Rogers was exceptional.

“You could see our identity and our togetherness and the way we managed the game,” said Le Bris, who was booked when hectoring referee Jarred Gillett. “These three points were critical. It was a struggle at times to manage situations. We showed as a group real heart.”

And nobody did that more than Brobbey. No wonder Le Bris will be hoping Xavi Hernández, the Netherlands head coach, handles him with care over the next 10 days. On this form, he will be the fuel that drives Sunderland’s quest for survival.

“You know when you come here in this stadium it will be a difficult game and that was the matter tonight. We knew it would be tough, we are disappointed we lost the game. At one point it went very fast from side to side. Sometimes we had to control. With 11 behind the ball it is difficult to find the spaces.”

On where Chelsea stand ahead of the international break...

“How you do – good or not – it is a matter of staying together. The international break is coming so the lads can be calm in the head and when we all come back we need to be motivated to go again.”

“For me it wasn’t a penalty. He barely touched him, I think it was the other way round. He grabbed him.”

They cannot make anything of set piece and Sunderland have the three points - it wasn’t pretty but they needed the three points and edged the contest.

Questions will be asked of Chelsea now, they were bullied in the first-half and weren’t able to create anything in the second.

Chelsea with the ball inside the Sunderland half. The visitors bring Rogers down and Chelsea have a free-kick. Last-chance sallon for the west Londoners...

Sunderland have a throw inside the Chelsea half - this is about game management for the side in dire need of a win now...

Angulo nrings down his man after a poor pass from Sadiki. The visitors with a free-kick inside their own half.

Emegha drifts past Mukiele before he feels the full force of a Luke O’Nein tackle. It looks as though he gets the ball but the ref awards the free-kick. It’s in the final third, can Chelsea create anything from this?

In short ‘yes’, Estevao delivers a peach of a ball and Welbeck gets on the end of it. BUT his header is over, when it seemed easier to hit the target.

Sunderland in Chelsea half, they’re looking for a free-kick as Angulo goes down. The referee isn’t having any of it...

Sunderland break at pace (only the second time this half) Isador finds Talbi who is free before cutting inside and unleashing a shot from outside the box. It’s just wide, don’t think it was too far away though.

Talbi is off for Angulo, Rigg on for Le Fee for Sunderland, and for Chelsea, Henderson makes way for Emegha.

For all their possession this half Chelsea have not forced Roefs into a meaningful save. The west Londoners are again dominating possession in and near the hinterland of the Sunderland box, but it’s all a bit after you Claude and ultimately Roefs gladly picks up an anaemic cross. That sums up Chelsea as an attacking force today.

Chelsea corner after Geovany Quenda gets in a shot from the left-side of the area that gets a tiny hint of a deflection. Roefs punches away the set-piece and Sunderland breathe a sigh of relief.

Better from Sunderland, there are spaces in behind Chelsea as the visitors go in search of the equaliser and over the past few minutes the hosts have found them.

Lovely ball from Reinildo finds Sadiki in space on the left, they keep the ball brilliantly before Le Fee plays in Isador, it’s a one-on-one and all the Frenchman has to do it dink it over the on-rushing keeper. He goes low, however, and Penders makes a fine save - that was the game for Sunderland there...Penders has kept Chelsea in this.

Brobbey may have been tiring but without him Sunderland cannot keep the ball. Sadiki earns a free-kick which takes a bit of pressure off the hosts.

Palmer pulls back for Gusto whose dinky, cheeky chip tries to find Roefs off his line. He doesn’t succeed and the Dutch goalkeeper claims with ease.

Chelsea still seeing plenty of the ball, Sunderland may well be tiring. It’s hard to keep up that intensity for 90 minutes, hence Isador on for Brobbey, but they are struggling to keep the ball at the moment.

The first half was lively and entertaining, this half has been lively and lacking in anything that could be remotely described as a spectacle...

Rogers tries to find Palmer, but the ball is too long and Roefs gobbles up with ease.

Meanwhile, Hume looks injured and Chelsea do not give the ball back after Sunderland kicked it off. You won’t be shocked to hear that the home fans are not happy with that...

Change for Sunderland, Brobbey off for Isador. The Dutchman has been brilliant today, he might have scored a couple of goals, but despite not finding the back of the net he has proved a handful for the Chelsea backline. I would have kept him on for longer...

Chelsea looking better this half, they’re seeing plenty of the ball but have not had a shot on goal since the break. In fact there have only been two touches in either box this 45...Sunderland won’t mind that at 1-0.

ON - Welbeck and GustoOFF - Neto and Palestra

So Alonso has opted for a physical presence up front.

No sooner had I pressed send on that last post than Chelsea break through the middle but some great last-ditch defending from Muenier prevents Estevao from getting a shot at goal.

Chelsea haven’t been able to play through Sunderland and you think they’d need to bring on a physical presence up front if that’s to change.

Another chance for Sunderland - they break down the right before Hume sends in a low ball to the penalty box, it’s met first time by Le Fee, I think, and Penders saves low to his right. To state the obvious, the hosts would love a second to give them a deserved cushion. As I typed that last but the linesman has his flag up, it wouldn’t have counted, promising signs nonetheless.

Pressure from Sunderland. A good bit of possession ends with Mukiele swinging in a lovely cross from the right which Chelsea are forced to head clear for a corner. Nothing results from the set piece, but things still looking promising for Sunderland who look as energetic and ‘at it’ as they did in the first half.

Rogers picks up the ball in the middle just inside the Sunderland half and is immediately pick-pocketed by one of three Sunderland players. The Chelsea men have not been allowed to settle when they have a sniff of a mini counter.

Good, feisty opening to this half, Chelsea look more up for it, though to be fair they couldn’t look any more insipid than they did in the first 45. Meanwhile, Brobbey shoves Lavia and earns a yellow. Think that’s three yellows for the hosts now.

It is going to be fascinating to see how a team with well known - and long standing - disciplinary issues copes with a pressurised pursuit of an equaliser. There have already been a couple of flash points that Chelsea’s players have reacted to and it wouldn’t be the wildest thing to predict referee Jarred Gillett brandishing a red card before the end of the game. Watch it unfold with interest.

Brobbey lays the ball off for Meunier in the final third, it’s asking a lot of the Belgian but his compounds the Dutchman’s error with one of his own - stretching for the ball and taking out Caicedo. Something for which he earns a needless yellow card.

There’s a bit of argy bargy on the pitch, not sure what started that but the referee Jarred Gillett has to have a word with several players. All a bit of handbags really.

They’re back under way on the banks of the Wear. Chelsea have been insipid and you imagine they won’t be as bed these next 45 minutes. Can Sunderland play with the same aggression and energy? We’re about to find out.

Changes Estevao on for Colwill, interesting substitution to say the least...

So close for Brobbey! 🤏 Sunderland almost take the lead against Chelsea. https://t.co/CUE6jHbPH2

The half ends with an audacious attempt at goal from Rogers, a full 40 yards out from a free kick. It’s catching practice for Roefs and that sums up Chelsea as an attacking force in the first 45. Sunderland are well worth their lead.

Rogers has a shot-cum-cross from the left and it sails high, wide and not so handsome. He’s been on the periphery this half, as has Palmer and that explains as much as anything why they are behind. Sunderland have cut out the supply to him and Roefs has had little to do as a result.

Approaching half-time and save for the contentious VAR call when he wanted a penalty, Cole Palmer has done absolutely nothing. The talk of him being in the England squad, on this evidence, is for the birds. Sunderland are full value for their half-time lead. Chelsea, like Palmer, have been absolutely insipid.

There will be five minutes added time in this first half.

Something I’ve not written much this half ‘chance for Chelsea’. Neto works a bit of space in the inside-right channel outside the box, but his shot is easily saved by Roefs.

Talbi attacks down the left but cuts in when he would have been better served going wide.

Chelsea have seen plenty of the ball but they’ve been way too slow and cumbersome with it. It’s been in front of the Sunderland back lines and easy to defend against. The hosts are letting the visitors have the ball wide and with Neto in the middle, it’s been too easy for Le Bris’s men.

Brobbey wants the ball at every opportunity and Sunderland would be well advised to give it to him. Colwill is has his hands full.

Sunderland have kept the aggression and energy throughout the half - and kept Chelsea quiet as a result. As I type that the hosts give Lavia too much room 25 yards out and his shot is well wide of the left-hand post.

The lead is no more than Sunderland deserve and that means, as the table stands, Manchester United are bottom of the Premier League. Fair play to Enzo Le Fee for keeping his nerve in a pressure situation. Sunderland needed him to be cool.

They’ve deserved that, they’ve been the better side and are well worth the lead. Le Fee sends Penders the wrong way, burying the ball into the bottom left corner.

Brobbey has been a handful (as he always is) and Colwill brings the BIG (yes, caps lock and bold are necessary) Dutchman down in the box. It looks as though it was six of one and hald a dozen of the other, but the spotkick stands.

Ahoka has impressed since coming on, his nifty footwork helps win Sunderland a throw in the final third. Mukiele has a big thrown on him but it does not result in a chance. Still, this is good from the hosts and Chelsea are second best at the moment. They were in the first half against United last week, and ended up winning so...

Another chance for Sunderland as Brobbey bullies Colwill on the halfway line before driving at Fofana. He gets to the edge of the area, beats the Chelsea defender before his shot goes wide. The last touch took him too wide, but again, promising signs for the hosts.

Early days this, of course, but Sunderland absolutely do not look like a team that is currently the worst in the Premier League. They should have the lead here but Brian Brobbey’s miss from six yards is indicative of how things have been going.

Sunderland are being aggressive, they need to be and it’s a contrast from the previous month. With that approach, however, comes risks and Mukiele gives away a free-kick inside his own half. Luckily for him, nothing comes from the set-piece.

First chance of the game for Chelsea and, as with Brobbey 10 minutes ago, it should have found the back of the net. Rogers is the culprit - he sends his header wide of the right post after a grade-A cross from Palestra.

One-all in terms of great chances...but the score remains 0-0.

Palmer is bundled over on the outskirts of the area and he and Chelsea players appeal for something - could be a free-kick of penalty...the referee is having nothing of it. The replay suggests he may well have been hard done by but VAR also is having nothing of it...it was a foul as none of the marauding Sunderland players, O’Nien among them (obviously), got the ball and most definitely got Palmer...think the hosts got away with that one.

Yellow card for Ahoka for a foul on Caicado, he may need to walk a tightrope for the rest of the match. But it’s an illustration of the energy and purpose with which Sunderland have approached this match.

Sunderland have looked the better side so far and have had the better chances.

Better from Chelsea in the sense that they controlled the game for two minutes. Lots of good, neat passing but no end product, it’s all in front of a composed Sunderland defence.

Another good chance for Sunderland and once again Talbi proves his worth. He cuts back onto his right and delivers a peach of a cross from the left. Brobbey gets in front of his man and all he has to do is hit the target...alas his first-time shot goes wide. That should be 1-0 to the hosts who are the better side at the moment.

Good from Sunderland who look so much more energetic than at any point during their previous few matches. Ahoka does well in the middle before freeing Talbi down the left. The Moroccan gets in a cross and Le Fee’s shot is blocked. Promising signs for the hosts.

What a blow this is for Regis Le Bris. Less than two minutes gone and Granit Xhaka is having to leave the pitch with an obvious injury. Some fans around the press box booed Xhaka as he was hobbling off - is that a hangover from his attempts to move to Chelsea? - but on afternoon when Le Bris needed everything to go his way, he’s already on the back foot.

Neto is in the Sunderland half but three Sunderland players snap at his heels like a hyperactive dog after a bone. Chelsea haven’t been allowed to settle yet. Plenty of time to go though...

Sunderland are looking to find Brobbey at every opportunity, but Chelsea’s backline intercept well. Nothing of note created so far, but the hosts are on the front foot, which is what they and the fans needed.

Sunderland attack down the right with Meunier, nothing comes of it but the hosts look as though they mean business here. A minute later Sadiki and Brobbey nearly combine to create something. Close but no cigar...

Bad news for Sunderland, Xhaka is down and it looks as though he may well have to come off...oh dear. While he’s not been at his best this season he’s still the man the side looks towards for inspiration (an boy do they need that is dollops today...)...and, indeed he is forced off. Ahoka, who is highly rated but raw replaces him. The Congolese player now has a big chance to make a name for himself.

Chelsea with the early possession, but they go backwards and the hosts are up and at them with the press and the visitors have to go back to Penders in goal.

They’re under way at the Stadium of Light, Sunderland are in their famous red and white and Chelsea in their away outfit of black shirts and shorts and yelow socks.

As the Stadium of Light remembers all those who lost their lives in war.

The Last Post is played and the minute’s silence is impeccably observed.

Warming-up in our Remembrance shirt ❤️ https://t.co/aTB8sfdLKP

And we’re moments away from kick-off in the North East.

This is a big afternoon for both teams. It will be an emotional one, too, for Jordan Henderson, who started his career at Sunderland many years ago. Xabi Alonso has confirmed he has been picked because of the quality he provides, rather than any sentimental value, and Regis Le Bris revealed ahead of the fixture he tried to bring the England international home during the summer window, when Chelsea attempted to sign Granit Xhaka.

“Jordan is a great player, first of all,” said Le Bris. “For the connection with the club, it’s not my part. It was with Flo [Ghisolfi, director of football] and Kyril [Louis-Dreyfus, the Sunderland owner], they had conversations.

“I thought that it could have been a good signing for the club, a good symbol, a great player, a great leader. But the market is the market.”

Has just said that Sunderland, and in particular Brian Brobbey, can ‘get at’ the Chelsea defence of Palestra, Fofana, Colwill, Chavarria. I am not sure he has seen much of the Sunderland attack this year, but Brobbey is a handful for any defence.

“We have to stay consistent and true to our identity. It’s always difficult to predict what the other side does but you have to focus on yourself and connect with the fans and impose our ideas.”

On whether they can get a result today...

“I hope so... I see the players every day, they care and sometime its hard to understand the unforced errors.”

“He’s loved by fans and team, so we know the situation at beginning of season. He is an important player for us and didn’t start for various reasons, but has qualities run in behind and finish - he’s excited worked and has worked hard.”

I mentioned earlier that Sunderland did the double over Chelsea last season. But the manner of the victories revealed more than the scorelines. In both matches, especially the second, the west Londoners looked somewhat lightweight and easily bullied.

This season Xabi Alonso has been determined to ensure that that is not the case this season.

In the land of the Premier League giants, Chelsea have been on the small side in recent seasons. But they are no longer being looked down upon and are finally showing signs of being capable of going toe-to-toe physically with opponents.

Sunday’s opponents Sunderland ran Chelsea off the park twice last season. Only once, in the 36th Premier League game of the campaign against Liverpool, did Chelsea cover more distance than their opposition.

Here’s Matt Law’s article on Why Chelsea have gone from pint-sized players to taller trees...

SUNDERLAND XI TO FACE CHELSEA: Roefs, Meunier, Mukiele, O’Nein, Reinildo, Xhaka, Hume, Le Fee, Talbi, Brobbey.

Subs: Ellborg, Danso, Methalie, Rigg, Tutierov, Ahoka, Fofana, Angulo, Isador

Regis Le Bris makes two changes from the sorry defeat at Coventry City. Nordi Mukiele returns to the centre of defence and there’s a start for Chemsdine Talbi  – Chris Rigg and Nilson Angulo are the ones to make way.

CHELSEA XI TO FACE SUNDERLAND: Penders, Palestra, Fofana, Colwill, Chavarria, Henderson, Lavia, Caicedo, Neto, Palmer, Rogers.

Subs: Sharman-Lowe, Gusto, Anselmino, Nicoll-Jazuli, Barco, Quenda, Estevao, Welbeck, Emegha.

Xabi Alonso also makes two changes – Pep Chavarria and Jordan Henderson start today. Estevao Willian drops to the bench while Josh Acheampong is a somewhat surprise absence the 20.

Goalkeeper Mike Penders continues in goal with Emiliano Martinez deemed not ready to return having fractured his jaw against Everton.

That Sunderland did the double over Chelsea last season.

A last-minute winner from Chemsdine Talbi grabbed the points at Stamford Bridge, before Sunderland won 2-1, without breaking sweat, at the Stadium of Light on the last day of the campaign.

Those victories, and the manner of them, underlined what a season it was for Regis Le Bris’s men. How they wish this campaign started as that one ended.

RLB's XI to take on Chelsea! 📝👊 #SUNCHE https://t.co/1XWyHk0x56

Your Chelsea side today! ✔️ #CFC | #SUNCHE https://t.co/ciaILJeAuu

For Sunderland that argument is easy to make – they are bottom of the Premier League, are without a win since August and for morale, if nothing else need at least a point, though three is really what the doctor orders.

For Chelsea – fourth in the table and with three wins in their past four league outings – the argument that this is a must-win game is harder to make, but bear with me here...

Facing a Sunderland team who are suffering from the worst of both worlds – blunt in attack and pitiful in defence (what a difference from last season...) and have proven all too easy to beat (as their 2-0 home defeat Zagreb illustrated on Thursday) – the west Londoners are expected to win. Fail to return to the capital with the three points and there will once again be question marks over Xabi Alonso’s side. They are flaky and flashy in equal measure, able to play and win well in spurts, but once again unable to mount sustained pressure needed for a title challenge and forced to battle it out for the hope of a top-four spot at best. Those will be the arguments raised should they not win this afternoon.

The hosts doubtless wish that their ‘issues’ were as golden as today’s opposition. For Trai Hume, who scored in this fixture last season, the Sunderland players are at fault for the sorry start to the season and he wants to put right the wrongs so far, starting today.

“I couldn’t tell you what’s changed. We thought we’d addressed it after the Leeds game, where we were aggressive, strong, but we go out there tonight and see the old habits of the start of the season. Everything’s a bit laboured, and it’s something the staff can’t fix, it’s on us as players,” Hume said.

“We’re still together as a club, as a team. I think the run of form we’re on, it would be easy to think we’re not, but we are. We are really upset with how we’ve been playing, and the results don’t lie. We haven’t been good enough and we know that. We have to address that.”

#1065. England's evolution: James Trafford and two other stars chisel their names into the XI, Thomas Tuchel learning from Argentina and Jude Bellingham playing like a captain!

Published: 02:32 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 09:25 EST, 16 November 2026

England ended world champions Spain's 43-match unbeaten run in dramatic fashion with a 3-2 win on a memorable night in Madrid.

After Harry Kane, Ezri Konsa and Ben White scored to establish a three-goal lead, the visitors had to cling on after Elliot Anderson was sent off and the hosts scored twice in the final half hour.

The victory means Thomas Tuchel's side top their Nations League group and it provided a strong riposte to criticism of the manager following the World Cup semi-final defeat by Argentina in July.

Our chief football reporter, Craig Hope, was at the Metropolitano Stadium, and here are his FIVE big take-aways…

It would not have mattered had England conceded a late equaliser. To draw comparison with Argentina in the final half hour is unfair and inaccurate. The World Cup semi-final was 11v11 and so, when we draw conclusions from this game, let us do so on the same terms.

Thomas Tuchel was delighted with his England players as they won 3-2 away in Spain

And what did England do at 11v11 with a 1-0 lead? They attacked. And attacked again. This was a major change (and improvement) and is the reason for such encouragement. They have learnt from a mistake, as much as Tuchel will be loathe to admit.

Mexico would be a fairer parallel, but that was against opposition far inferior to Spain. At 11v10, we could not expect England to stay on the front foot here, as they were until the point of Jarell Quansah's needless mistake and Elliot Anderson's subsequent red card.

And that is cause for great optimism - because this game was not in the balance in any way when the teams were at equal number.

For me, and I don't think this is even close, this was the best performance of Tuchel's reign.

Do England suddenly have a pair of full backs?! After years of trawling and trialling, here in the most testing of surrounds, Ben White and Lewis Hall inked their names into Tuchel's XI.

We can forgive the concession of two goals when down to 10 men - because with 11, Spain barely looked like getting a shot on target. In fact, they didn't.

Much of that was down to the solidity of the full backs. Then, with backs to the wall, the pair became bricks in the resistance. One White block late on was heroic.

Before that, Hall's best work was not in containing Lamine Yamal, but in emulating him. His dribbles were daring and unnerved Spain, who thought they would spend the game in England's half and with the ball. They did neither early on and Hall was central to that.

White's goal had shades of Carlos Alberto on the overlap, and his England redemption arc felt like it reached completion here. Let him now move on now, for England need him.

No more boos, please, only cheers for White (and Hall).

It's time to stop the boos for Ben White after he starred with Lewis Hall at full back

Ezri Konsa is England's best defender. Build the backline around him.

Tuchel said on the eve of the game that he thought Konsa had grown for the move to Arsenal, and this was proof.

Boy do England need a mature, reliable presence at the heart of their defence. Konsa showed here why he can be that man. He scored a fine goal, which is always a sign of a defender ready to take wider responsibility, but it was his cool interceptions and desperate blocks at the other end that were most reassuring.

What Konsa has to do now is build on this - and a man-of-the-match performance at the home of the world champions is a pretty lofty and solid foundation from which to do so.

Tuchel will, and should, be giving serious thought to keeping James Trafford in England's goal for the Nations League quarter-finals.

Jordan Pickford has done nothing wrong. And yet, it feels like one position the manager wants to evolve - and here was his justification.

Trafford can be a little erratic and immature. What better way to grow, emotionally, than with a series of saves to preserve an historic win. He will feel like a different player, and person, to the one who started this game. Like White and Hall, this felt like a coming-of-age night in an England jersey.

Trafford has all the tools. He might just have used them to chisel his name into that team-sheet.

Goalkeeper feels like one position the manager wants to evolve - and James Trafford starred

Spain's fans are left shocked as Ezri Konsa hails the brilliant Trafford in emphatic fashion

No goals, but England would not have won this game without Bellingham. He terrified Spain, perhaps given their intimate knowledge of his brilliance.

Beating the best is as much a mental challenge as it is physical, and Bellingham believed. He made England believe, too.

His swagger. His majesty. And yes, his skill. Of all the positives from this win, it is hard to look past Bellingham as the biggest reason for England being able to challenge Spain at the top of the world rankings.

Jude Bellingham played like a captain, dropping into midfield when down to 10 men

He won the corner for the second goal and created the third. He then dropped into midfield when down to 10 and played like a captain.
