#1064. Spain v England player ratings: White silences doubters as Trafford makes case for No 1

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Spain 2-3 England: Thomas Tuchel’s men clung on despite going down to 10 men to end Spain’s 43-game unbeaten run

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

England clung on to beat Spain 3-2 and top Nations League Group A3 in a thriller in Madrid, inflicting the first defeat on the world champions at home in 39 years.

Harry Kane deservedly opened the scoring with a composed penalty shortly before half-time, before Ezri Konsa doubled the Three Lions’ lead in the second half with a free header from a Declan Rice corner.

Ben White then marked his full return to the England fold - having started for the first time in this campaign - with a brilliant finish through Simon’s legs to make it 3-0.

But the game flipped entirely when Elliot Anderson was sent off and conceded a penalty for hauling down Lamine Yamal 65 minutes in, with Mikel Oyarzabal slotting home the spot-kick to make it 3-1.

Anthony Gordon was punished for losing possession cheaply as Yamal raced away to tee up Nico Williams for Spain’s second, setting up a grandstand finish in Madrid.

James Trafford was the hero as he produced several fine saves, including a double in extra time, and England held on to make a major statement and end Spain’s 43-game unbeaten run.

Here is how the players rated at the Metropolitano:

James Trafford, 8: Had absolutely nothing to do until the second half as Spain failed to have a shot on target, then did his hopes of becoming England’s No 1 no harm at all despite Spain’s two goals. Great reflex save to deny Fermin Lopez in the 73rd minute and a fine double save from Marc Cucurella 80 minutes in, then another superb double save to deny Lopez and Yamal in extra time.

Ben White, 9: At the centre of England’s fast, aggressive start; won the corner which nearly led to a second-minute opener and drilled a fine finish through Unai Simon’s legs for the third goal, then made a crucial late block to deny Lamine Yamal. Bit of needless argy-bargy with Fabian Ruiz at half-time but did well to silence those who booed him on his England return. Replaced by Dan Burn for the final few minutes.

Ezri Konsa, 9: Part of a composed and solid back line and marked his return to action with a lovely header from a corner to double England’s lead early in the second half.

Jarell Quansah, 8: Conceded a free-kick with a block on Cucurella but was otherwise solid in defence.

Lewis Hall, 9: Superb: industrious and composed in defence, bringing an end to a dangerous Spain counter shortly before half-time, leading the way in dribbles and winning duels, and kept Yamal quiet. Contributed to England’s attack too; made an excellent mazy run through the box 18 minutes in, but there was no one in space to receive his cross.

Elliot Anderson, 5: Solid in midfield for 60 minutes and produced a terrific long pass to Kane which led to the captain winning the penalty, but sent off and conceded a penalty for hauling Yamal down in the box with the Spaniard through on goal, which entirely transformed the game.

Jude Bellingham, 8: Unlucky to be denied an early opener with an excellent attempt, then hit the side-netting 25 minutes in. Combined well with Kane and was at the centre of every England move, then was unhappy to be withdrawn for Dominic Calvert-Lewin late on.

Declan Rice, 7: Conceded a needless free-kick and yellow card for tripping Yamal, and sent a poor free-kick straight at Simon in the 34th minute. Redeemed himself with an excellent delivery for Konsa’s goal and was a physical presence in midfield.

Morgan Rogers, 6: Didn’t quite get the pass right to Bellingham after a fine first-half team move. Outshone by the rest of the attack tonight.

Harry Kane, 8: In the right positions but flashed an early chance narrowly wide and off-target with a close-range header which was flagged offside. But led the line as always, won the penalty and put England in front with a brilliantly composed spot-kick. Replaced by Myles Lewis-Skelly.

Anthony Gordon, 6: A tale of two halves: 9 for the first half, 4 for the second. Fast and relentless; had the beating of Marc Pubill for pace and was a constant threat down the left flank. Let himself down by conceding possession cheaply and was punished by Lamine Yamal for Spain’s second, then hauled off shortly after for Djed Spence.

Unai Simon, 7: Called into action right from the start with a superb goal-line clearance to deny Bellingham. Kept busy throughout and made some good saves but was embarrassed by Ben White scoring through his legs.

Marc Pubill, 5: Struggled to keep pace with England’s attackers and only made a brief cameo, replaced 20 minutes in by Pedro Porro after colliding heavily with Unai Simon.

Pau Cubarsi, 4: Showed little of his usual magic. Responsible for conceding a penalty with a poor last-ditch challenge on Kane shortly before half-time, getting none of the ball and all of the man. Replaced by Dean Huijsen at the break.

Aymeric Laporte, 7: Consistent at the back, especially in the second half.

Marc Cucurella, 7: Bothered England with some nippy fouls and won a cheap free-kick in the first half-hour, but his dramatics - arguing he was fouled by Anderson in the build-up to England winning the penalty - weren’t enough to have it chalked off.

Martin Zubimendi, 6: Crowded out and constantly under pressure in midfield, but improved in the second half. Replaced by Nico Williams 72 minutes in.

Fabian Ruiz, 7: Produced a dangerous curling cross into the box which was one of Spain’s best chances of the first half-hour, but denied by the England defence. Involved in a scrap at half-time with Ben White and did not return at the restart.

Lamine Yamal, 9: Kept quiet in the early stages but grew into the contest and was key to Spain’s press as they started to trouble England. Was essentially the only attacking threat Spain had for 60 minutes, won the penalty off Anderson, and set up Williams for Spain’s second with a beautiful pass.

Mikel Merino, 5: Entirely anonymous and hooked for Pedri at half-time.

Alex Baena, 8: Sent a dangerous cross into the area after Yamal was fouled by Rice in a rare attacking foray by Spain in a listless first half. Combined well with Yamal throughout.

Mikel Oyarzabal, 8: Sent Trafford the wrong way to score Spain’s 65th minute penalty for 3-1 and turned the game on its head.

Pedro Porro: 8; Dean Huijsen: 7; Fermin Lopez: 9; Pedri: 8; Nico Williams: 9.

#1062. Thomas Tuchel offers verdict in battle for England’s No 1 spot after landmark win over Spain

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

James Trafford came into the starting line-up in place of Jordan Pickford as England secured a famous win in Madrid

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

England manager Thomas Tuchel refused to get drawn into debates around his starting goalkeeper after James Trafford helped the Three Lions to a famous win over Spain in Madrid.

Tuchel’s side put on a superb display at the Riyadh Air Metropolitano, with Harry Kane opening the scoring from the spot before Ezri Konsa broke free to nod in from a corner when unmarked early into the second half.

The Three Lions were in dreamland not long after, with a superb team goal ending with Ben White sliding an accomplished finish in for 3-0 in the 58th minute.

However, the game changed just after the hour mark, with Elliot Anderson bringing down Lamine Yamal as the last man. The England midfielder was sent off, and Mikel Oyarzabal scored his spot-kick to get Spain back into it.

It felt like groundhog day for England as Nico Williams scored a second for La Roja in the 75th minute, though the Three Lions clung on to secure a 3-2 win, inflicting the world champions’ first defeat in 43 games.

And while Trafford had little to do before the red card, he was called into action plenty of times in the final stages of the game, making several important stops.

Nevertheless, Tuchel was coy when asked whether the youngster’s performance was enough to make him England’s no. 1.

“There’s no number one. It’s a good double save. That’s what we wanted. He had a brilliant match. It only works if you’re top from number one to 11,” said Tuchel after full-time.

Tuchel was referencing two brilliant late stops from Trafford to deny Fermin Lopez and Lamine Yamal in stoppage time. The latter particularly stood out, with the Leeds keeper recovering from the first stop in a matter of seconds to get across and tip the rebound past the post.

Trafford’s display will fuel debate over whether he should take Jordan Pickford’s place as England’s starting goalkeeper, with eyebrows raised when Tuchel decided to drop the Everton keeper ahead of facing the world champions.

Pickford has previously been the undisputed choice in goal and the veteran started England’s last three games, though it was Trafford who was in goal at Wembley for the 3-2 loss to Spain in September, as well as for the win over Czechia a few days later.

In any case, it gives Tuchel a welcome selection headache, and we are likely to discover who the German sees as his number one in March when the Nations League quarter-finals take place.

England’s win means they finished top of Group A3, and they will face one of the second-placed teams in the next round, with the likes of Belgium, the Netherlands, Germany and Denmark potentially waiting in the last eight.

The draw for the next round takes place on Friday, 20 November, with the matches taking place between 25 and 30 March 2027.

#1061. Romelu Lukaku announces 'bombshell' international retirement: Former Chelsea star, 33, U-turns on his Belgium future - leaving Belgian press stunned

By BEN WILLCOCKS, ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR

Published: 08:03 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 09:49 EST, 16 November 2026

Romelu Lukaku has announced his retirement from international football in a 'bombshell' decision that has left the Belgian press utterly stunned.

The former Chelsea and Manchester United forward, 33, vowed in January that the 2026 World Cup would not be his last major tournament with the Belgium national team, although he now appears to have changed his mind over his future.

Describing his international career as a 'great ride', Lukaku took to social media on Monday morning to break the unexpected news.

'16 years old,' his Instagram statement began. 'For 16 years, I gave everything for the national team. I experienced every possible emotion. I played with fantastic teammates for whom I will always be grateful.

'I want to thank them all. I also want to thank all the coaches for pushing me and giving me the confidence to help the team. It was a great ride, and I enjoyed every moment.

'To the Belgian fans, thank you for the support you have given our team. I am proud to have represented my country at four World Cups and three European Championships. I will never forget those moments. I am at peace with my decision to stop here. It was amazing, it was a joy. I am grateful. Thank you.'

Belgium legend Romelu Lukaku has announced his decision to retire from international football

Lukaku vowed in January that the 2026 World Cup would not be his last major tournament

The Belgian forward has fallen down the pecking order and spent a lot of time on the bench

The Belgian veteran accompanied his post with a gallery of photographs from his storied international career, from his debut against Croatia under Dick Advocaat in 2010 to his final chapter wearing the armband.

Lukaku has captained Belgium on a handful of occasions since 2020, alongside the likes of Kevin De Bruyne and Youri Tielemans.

The 33-year-old forward, who became one of the hottest properties in world football after breaking on the scene at Chelsea, has been a regular fixture in the international set-up for almost two decades.

Spearheading Belgium's golden generation, which included star-studded talents such as De Bruyne, Thibaut Courtois and Eden Hazard, Lukaku chalked up an impressive 135 caps for the international team.

He also retires as Belgium's all-time top scorer on 94 goals, just six shy of a century.

Belgian newspapers were caught out by the shock announcement, which was described as an 'unexpected bombshell' by outlet HLN on Monday.

Lukaku's stock within the international set-up has fallen since he promised the 2026 World Cup would not be his last major tournament in January.

After suffering multiple injury setbacks, he featured at the tournament under Rudi Garcia and continued to play a crucial role, scoring three times as a substitute to guide Belgium to the quarter-finals where they were ultimately stopped by eventual champions Spain.

Since Mark van Bommel's appointment in August, following Garcia's departure at the end of his contract, Lukaku has slipped further down the pecking order, with Charles De Ketelaere preferred to lead the line.

Lukaku, pictured with Kevin De Bruyne, was an unused substitute as Belgium beat Italy 4-1

Axel Witsel sent a heartfelt message to Lukaku on Instagram: 'Thanks for everything, legend'

During Belgium's resounding 4-1 victory over Italy on Sunday, Lukaku warmed the bench as an unused substitute - and wasn't even in the squad to face Turkey three days before.

While Belgium were winning in the second half against the Italians, Lukaku was seen warming up on the sidelines in the hope of featuring for one last time, but unfortunately was not given the opportunity.

VTM NIEUWS anchor Maarten Breckx claimed De Bruyne looked 'concerned' while speaking to Lukaku on the bench, suggesting the former Man City star was unhappy to see his team-mate overlooked.

'When it became clear that he wouldn't be allowed to come on, De Bruyne was talking to him. You could see the concern in his eyes,' he said.

'You could tell, especially from Romelu's attitude, that he was dissatisfied and displeased. He had probably counted on getting some minutes...'

With only Jan Vertonghen and Axel Witsel registering more international caps than Lukaku over their careers, boasting 157 and 140 appearances respectively, Belgium are expected to give the 33-year-old forward a send-off he deserves in the near future.

Witsel, who also called time on his Belgium career this year, was one of the team-mates to celebrate Lukaku's retirement on Instagram.

'Thanks for everything, legend. Thank you, what a journey we've had together,' he wrote.

#1060. Arsenal make no sense – and defiant Mary Earps proves why

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Arsenal 1-1 London City Lionesses: The Gunners drew at the Emirates for the fifth game in a row as Izzy Goodwin cancelled out Frida Maanum’s opener after just 98 seconds

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Alone in an empty penalty box, Mary Earps dropped to her knees and yelled into the cold night air. With an eight-save, player-of-the-match display, the ‘Queen of Stops’ properly marked the end of her exile and return to the Women’s Super League with an outstanding performance between the posts for the London City Lionesses in their 1-1 draw with Arsenal, a reminder to anyone who needed it that the former England No 1 is not done yet.

“Tiring,” Earps exhaled when asked to sum up a night where she did it all, including a sensational late stop to tip Frida Maanum’s dipping strike onto the bar and earn her side a point. There was agility, presence, bravery, but how about the timing, as well, to produce such a performance in front of the biggest crowd of the season at the Emirates and keep the disrupters London City above Arsenal in the race for the Champions League positions. In front of Sarina Wiegman, too.

But Earps and London City also managed to ensure that Arsenal’s miserable wait without a home win this season continued, with five successive draws at the Emirates to begin their campaign. It will be little consolation to Renee Slegers that her side showed more intent and direction that in their previous draws against Crystal Palace, Manchester United, Birmingham City and Aston Villa this season: this was billed as a must-win for Arsenal and the sight of the goalkeeper Misa Rodriguez going forward for a corner in the final seconds of stoppage time, at 1-1, revealed as much.

That Arsenal’s corner failed to even reach the box, with Smilla Holmberg’s outswinging delivery instead drifting out of play, summed up how perplexing their season has become. A team who started the season with title aspirations, to go along with the club’s wider ambitions, are left sitting sixth in the WSL after 10 games, 12 points off leaders Chelsea and six points off London City, the holders of the final Champions League place. Arsenal are simultaneously a team capable of going to Barcelona and the Camp Nou on Wednesday and drawing 1-1, while also failing to register a victory in front of the biggest women’s football crowd in the country in the last six months.

In a way, London City were the sort of opponents Arsenal should have enjoyed facing. The plucky upstarts, with the billionaire owner and Ballon d’Or holder in midfield, are expansive in possession and have interesting ideas about what to do on the ball. They arrived at the Emirates with a plan and ambition to do more than just nullify their opponents and it was a measure of their ability to dictate that Arsenal, at times, did not even attempt to press. London City had more possession and more passes, which for Arsenal at least allowed them to break out of the sterile, side-to-side patterns of play that had defined their previous stalemates here.

And there was a reminder, too, that Arsenal can be dangerous when they are presented with space, to attack in a way where they can move up the pitch and have a shot within seconds. Earps was kept busy, after all, and a lot of Arsenal managed to find made sense, at last: using Alessia Russo’s ability to work the channels and her awareness to bring others into play, looking to release Lisa Baum on the right and instructing her to be direct when she had a clear line to goal.

Maanum’s goal, after just 10 minutes, was an example of that. Emily Fox was invited to drive forwards and was directed to find Russo’s bending run off the shoulder of the last defender. There was a synchronisation to the way Russo didn’t even need to look up to know that Maanum would be arriving on the edge of the box, if she could find the right angle on the pull-back. There was a sense to Slegers leaving Olivia Smith and many of her summer signings on the bench and trusting the understanding between players like Russo and Maanum.

But then Arsenal this season have usually displayed a way of shooting themselves in the foot, too. As Maanum celebrated and her team-mates huddled around her, Leah Williamson was pointing to her head and telling them they still needed to stay switched on. Yet within 98 seconds London City were level due to a moment, a glitch in the system. It came from Williamson, failing to match Izzy Goodwin’s run, stepping in at the wrong time in the box. The England captain was horribly bypassed by a centre-forward who offered a sharp contrast by simply being in total control of what she was doing.

The frustration from Arsenal is their errors keep piling on top of each other, the scrutiny too. It is now just three wins from 10 in the WSL. Earps, in her defiance, sensed her opportunity to ensure there would be no respite.

#1059. Man Utd are in relegation trouble and Carrick must be sacked

Michael Carrick stood perfectly still and raised his left arm, and his index finger, high in the air. Around him, chaos. As it had been all afternoon. Substitute Patrick Dorgu had just headed in a corner to rescue a point for Manchester United in the 96th minute and, maybe, save Carrick his job.

Going into added time and United were two goals behind. It seemed all was lost for them against Aston Villa and for their head coach, but how telling was the reaction, in the directors’ box, of chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox, who both jumped up in celebration? They were far more animated than Carrick and could not contain themselves.

"Football is a contact sport!" 🗣️ Did Senne Lammens foul Zion Suzuki for Man United's equaliser? 🤔 https://t.co/KCb1lHqPHP

Did their behaviour betray not just their excitement in the moment but their relief at not having to sack Carrick during this forthcoming international break? If so, they need to think again. They need to make a sober and rational decision based on evidence. And the evidence shows that Carrick must go. Because this kind of football is unsustainable. This kind of football does not work. This kind of football is stupid.

United are 18th in the Premier League. They have won one game in 10 in the league. They have conceded 15 goals in their last five matches in the league and Champions League. When they play Liverpool away, their next game, on November 22, it will be the first time they have done so from inside the relegation zone since March 1937.

They appear shockingly disorganised. Tactics seem to be an after-thought, their motivation is lacking until desperation kicks in. United conceded two goals within four minutes at the start of the game. And then two more within eight minutes of the second half kicking off.

The bottom line is this: can they afford not to make a change? If they do not, United could be accused of copping out and gambling with their status. So, Berrada and Wilcox must ask: what is Carrick doing in the dressing room and on the training ground? What messages are he and his assistant Steve Holland sending out? Are the players even listening?

At the end the fans sang Carrick’s name after United became the first team in the Premier League to come back twice from being two goals down. That also summed up the fog of confusion at a club who so obviously lack direction – from the top down – and need to get a grip of themselves. Carrick talked about having to “tighten up” the defending. But everything needs to be stronger. More taut. More competitive.

Chaos can be entertaining. Chaos can be fun. As an advert for the Premier League this was outstanding. United fans will be thrilled with the Fergie-time comeback. But chaos is also unsustainable. No one knows what to expect from United.

In the cold light of day Villa manager Unai Emery will have to ask himself whether he, too, got it wrong. His substitutions did not work, bizarrely taking off too much experience, such as his outstanding captain John McGinn, and he handed United a late initiative when it looked like all hope was lost.

Michael Carrick has insisted he remains the right man to lead Manchester United and will not walk away despite the club being marooned in the relegation zone.

United came from 2-0 and 4-2 down to claim a last-gasp 4-4 draw against Aston Villa on another wild day at Old Trafford.It means United still only have one Premier League win to their name this season and are languishing in 18th position, a point adrift of safety, heading into the international break when the Old Trafford hierarchy must decide whether to keep faith with Carrick or appoint their third manager this year.

Carrick cut a spiky figure when asked about his future by Sky Sports and whether he would walk away.

“That’s not going to happen,” Carrick said, before asking “will there?” when it was put to him that there would “clearly” be conversations about his future.

“We haven’t won enough games, but I expect to move forward and keep working on the things we’ve been working on and showing a lot of good in the game today,” he said. “Tighten up on some things and start winning football matches.”

With four Premier League games in progress the picture is ever-changing, but United are currently 19th in the Premier League table. The club, famously, were relegated in 1974 with the coup de grâce applied by Denis Law’s backheel when the Scot was playing in a City shirt. In this piece, James Ducker looks back on the previous occasions when one of the world’s biggest clubs has flirted with calamity.

When Villa dropped into the Championship, it did not change the fact they were the biggest club in the Midlands. No matter what Tom Brady does at Birmingham City, that’s not changing any time soon. They sought and achieved promotion by raiding Brentford.

Nobody was complaining about a sleeping giant taking Dean Smith, Ezri Konsa or Ollie Watkins and potentially stalling Brentford’s progression.

Nor was it suggested hiring Emery from Villarreal was an odd move given that the Spanish side had recently won the Europa League and reached the latter stages of the Champions League.

#1058. How England found a new edge to beat Spain and exorcise agony of Argentina defeat

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Spain 2-3 England: Thomas Tuchel’s men clung on despite going down to 10 men to end Spain’s 43-game unbeaten run

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

England hold out, for a raucous win that will rightly be held up. Sure, it might not have been what it could have been as Ben White surged in for a sensational third in Madrid… but that last word remains key.

England beat the world and European champions 3-2 in their own capital, to end the longest unbeaten run in international history, that stretched back to March 2024.

Spain couldn’t make it 44 games, as England just about made it to 94 minutes. That was ultimately down to a brilliant double save from James Trafford, who was one of many positives on another Nations League night of enjoyably entertaining drama. Might Jordan Pickford’s first place have gone with Spain’s unbeaten run?

Trafford had to show his best. This was never going to be easy, no matter how Thomas Tuchel’s side made it look for 63 minutes - until Elliot Anderson’s red card. That will be the manager’s main takeaway from the game, the “proof of concept” as he put it the night before. With 11 against 11, England were denying this Spanish team the ball and creating some swift chances that the world champions were struggling to live with.

That was what the game-opening goal came from. Even if there was also debate about Anderson’s follow-through in that instance, England had opened another gap in the Spanish structure while looking so more cohesive and coruscating themselves.

This is a team that can sustain attacking waves much better than the one who mostly forced their way through the summer on individual impact. White’s supreme goal, that had the world champions looking at each other and pointing fingers, was the grand exhibition of that.

Just as crucially, it was so different to what Spain do. It was something of England's own. In between, Ezri Konsa scored the plundered set-piece header that his recent performances have deserved. Jude Bellingham was at that point bossing the Spanish midfield, in the kind of way people have long imagined as his career has only escalated.

This, and the very confidence from such a marker of a win, are what England have to take through to finally win that trophy at Euro 2028.

So many positives, so many solutions… until Spain asked the most severe questions, and Tuchel didn’t always have the answers. That is where there is obvious context to a win that should still inspire confidence.

It clearly meant much more to England given the fact Spain are the world champions who had won at Wembley. They're the ones who have done it, the benchmark. Tuchel and all the players were aware they had to do something more, to close this year with a performance that offered more for the future; that they had to stand up.

They had admittedly felt frustration from that Wembley defeat; that they could have won. As a consequence, England just looked sharper for pretty much all of the first hour. Spain didn’t even have a shot on target in the first half, as Unai Simon immediately had to withstand an England flurry.

The world champions weren’t counter-pressing in the way they were in the summer. England were starting to overrun them. The ultimate expression of that, in White’s goal, did seem to spark something in response.

It is possible that England themselves even got a bit overconfident. In what has been a theme in this double of games - that ended 3-2 apiece but see England top the group on goal difference - Tuchel’s side gave the ball away for a Spanish goal.

This time it was Anthony Gordon, who seemed to forget what Lamine Yamal can do. Even the Barcelona playmaker took a poor touch from there, leading to what felt like a needless challenge from Anderson. He was sent off, and Spain were set off.

It was immediately a different game. Spain were doing everything they weren’t in the first half. A change of midfield helped, with Fermin Lopez offering the impetus that Luis De La Fuente’s midfield had been missing. Nico Williams’s brilliant finish from an utterly sensational Yamal pass was then a goal to match White’s.

And so, in what was almost humorous irony, England ended 2026 in the way they’d ended its defining games: backs to the wall, a backline of nine, Tuchel hauling off his best attackers, and questions about the subs.

Spain really pressed. Yamal was at the heart of every move, creating almost every chance. The game then seemed to just constantly be the ball being fired across the England box. England were probably one bad bounce away from another inquest about Tuchel’s substitutions, and how he manages these matches.

But that bounce didn’t come. The equaliser didn't come. England stood up.

And that might be because of a decision Tuchel doesn’t even have to make. Trafford made his claim. England made their mark.

Tuchel has ultimately overseen their most significant win for some time, at least as regards what it means for finally winning that trophy. That’s what all this is about, after all.

Spain can fairly say that what really matters is what happens in tournaments, but it didn’t feel meaningless as they toiled to keep that unbeaten record and the Madrid crowd willed them on. That run is now over. Might that finally signal that this could be England’s time?

It is far too early to say, but this was the end to the year Tuchel wanted. It was the performance England needed.

#1056. Even giant anteaters in remote Brazil have microplastics in their blood

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Gemma Conroy is a freelance journalist in Mexico City and editor of Nature Briefing: Careers.

Giant anteaters traipsing across Brazil’s pristine wetlands and savannahs have ingested traces of plastic pollutants. Credit: Sylvain Cordier/Gamma-Rapho via Getty

Some of Brazil’s wildlife have traces of plastic circulating in their blood — even if they live far from land used by humans, according to an analysis published on 11 November in Nature1.

Researchers measured the concentration of microplastics in the blood of 47 animals: 26 lowland tapirs (Tapirus terrestris) and 21 giant anteaters (Myrmecophaga tridactyla). The scientists found that, on average, the creatures carry similar levels of plastic as many humans — roughly 74 particles per millilitre of blood. The animals that lived closest to human infrastructure and waste-management facilities had the highest levels of microplastics in their blood.

But even those living more than 100 kilometres from a waste sites and 65 kilometres from human infrastructure showed traces of the pollutants. This indicates that plastics can reach wildlife living far from where the pollution originates, says study co-author Marcia de Almeida Monteiro Melo Ferraz, a conservation scientist at the University of British Columbia’s Okanagan campus in Kelowna, Canada.

The findings are an important step to better understand how the particles impact wildlife, says Sofia Ya-Hsuan Liou, a geochemist at the National Taiwan University in Taipei.

Microplastics are tiny particles (smaller than five millimetres across) with many different chemical compositions. They can travel through the environment in rainwater, rivers and the atmosphere. Although several studies have measured microplastics levels in wildlife, few have explored how the surrounding environment influences what animals ingest, says study co-author Michael Noonan, a quantitative ecologist at the University of British Columbia’s Okanagan campus.

To find out, Noonan, Ferraz and their colleagues collected and analysed blood samples from animals living across the Amazon rainforest, the Cerrado savannah and the huge and pristine Pantanal wetland between February 2021 and November 2022. The researchers also used GPS data to track the animals’ movements and their exposure to a human footprint.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03660-5

Ferraz, M. A. M. M. et al. Nature https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11285-x (2026).

Thomas Tuchel’s side are guaranteed a place in the last eight after an impressive run including beating world champions Spain to top the group

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

England produced a statement win over world champions Spain in Madrid in their final Nations League group stage game to top group A3.

The Three Lions had already confirmed their place in the quarter-finals in March with victory over Croatia earlier in this window, but have given themselves the best chances of a favourable draw by beating Spain 3-2 on Sunday and proven they are one of the teams to beat.

Thomas Tuchel’s side will be glued to next Friday’s draw, with League A still to be completed across the international break.

But here’s everything you need to know about the next stages of the competition:

The draw will take place at 11am GMT on Friday 20 November.

England will feature in the last eight of the Nations League 2026/27, with a two-legged tie to decide who will play in the semi-finals and final, both to be played across a ‘finals’ week.

As well as the Nations League quarter-finals, the League A/B and League B/C promotion/relegation play-offs will be drawn, set to be held in March 2027. While the final tournament is scheduled to take place across 9–13 June 2027.

England's potential opponents in the last eight of the Uefa Nations League as things stand are Belgium, Greece or Denmark.

Beating Spain ensured the Three Lions will face a second-placed team in their quarter-final; Belgium have finished second in their group, while Greece could be pipped by Germany and Denmark could still be replaced by either Norway or Portugal.

England topping the group also means they will play the second leg of their quarter-final at home.

Newcastle United sit in mid-table after 10 games this season but the picture could be a whole lot bleaker by the New Year

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Sitting bottom of the Premier League’s Expected Points (xPTS) table is cause for concern at St James' Park this season.

Newcastle United’s high-risk tactical approach under new head coach Matthias Jaissle has left them exposed in transition, but their biggest structural weakness appears when they are forced onto the back foot. The team has largely relied on a single way of playing so far, with little in the way of an effective direct outlet when opponents pin them deep.

The root of the issue is highlighted in data published by Twitter/X user @markrstats who has examined how Premier League forwards perform when contesting long balls. The data visualisation plots volume (how often a forward is first to a long clearance per 90 minutes) against security (how often the forward's team retains possession).

Across the division, Newcastle’s attacking options register some of the weakest numbers in the league.

Matias Fernandez-Pardo ranks lowest in the below dataset for ball retention. While he contests an average of 2.8 long balls per 90 minutes, Newcastle retain possession following his involvement just 27% of the time. In practical terms, roughly three out of every four long balls targeted toward Fernandez-Pardo result in a turnover of possession.

Brian Brobbey is the best target man in the Premier League this season When Sunderland go long from their own half and he gets to the ball first, they keep it 79% of the time. The average for forwards is 53%. Calvert-Lewin, who wins far more long balls, is at 53%, Delap at 38% https://t.co/Q5Ftm51HOxNovember 8, 2026

Yoane Wissa offers even less presence in these situations. The DR Congo forward is first to just 1.2 long balls per 90 minutes - the lowest of any forward evaluated in the graphic.

His retention rate of roughly 41.5% is an improvement on Fernandez-Pardo, but his low involvement means Newcastle rarely look in his direction when clearing the ball from deep.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

By comparison, effective direct outlets offer either high-volume contesting or a high level of security. Dominic Calvert-Lewin contests 7.1 long balls per 90 for Leeds United, with a 53% retention rate, while Sunderland’s Brian Brobbey combines 4.9 long balls per 90 with a league-leading 79% retention rate.

Newcastle possess neither attribute in their current starting frontline.

This lack of aerial presence can leave the side trapped in their own half whenever an opposing press successfully cuts off short passing options - which is not a place any team wants to find themselves. Without a forward who can pin a centre-back or win an initial duel, Newcastle cannot move up the pitch as a unit.

Newcastle's squad does, however, contain a profile capable of addressing this shortcoming in Will Osula.

Standing at well over 6ft tall, the Danish international offers the physical profile Newcastle are currently missing centrally.

In his Premier League minutes, Osula has averaged 4.35 successful aerial duels per 90 - the highest among all Newcastle players, ahead of central defenders Dan Burn (4.00) and Sven Botman.

His aerial duel success rate regularly exceeds 70%, offering the target man traits required to bring supporting runners into play.

When he has started this season, Newcastle have looked more of a threat, including in the season opener at home to Liverpool, and the 2-0 away win against Crystal Palace.

Playing exclusively through transition and pressing is not yet generating reliable results for the Magpies. Unless Newcastle change their attacking style and deploy more of a reference point like Osula to make long balls stick, their lack of a direct alternative could drag them into a relegation fight.

#1050. Harry Kane explains why Spain ‘couldn’t live with’ England after stunning win in Madrid

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The reigning world and European champions were outplayed and then outfought by Thomas Tuchel’s side

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Harry Kane believes England’s victory in Spain is "as big as it gets" away from major tournaments, proving that even the best sides cannot cope with the assertive style developed since their World Cup near miss.

An intense year concluded in striking fashion on Sunday evening in Madrid, where the reigning world and European champions were outplayed and outfought by Thomas Tuchel’s hungry players.

Kane’s penalty earned England a deserved half-time lead, but they pressed on rather than beating a retreat as they had done during their costly World Cup semi-final collapse against Argentina.

Ezri Konsa and Ben White extended the lead, and Kane is confident more goals would have followed were it not for Elliot Anderson’s sending off, which allowed Mikel Oyarzabal and Nico Williams to reduce the deficit.

Spain pushed until the very end, but England demonstrated the resolve seen in July’s 3-2 last-16 win in Mexico, triumphing by the same scoreline to top their Nations League group in memorable fashion.

“I think that’s as big as it gets outside of a major tournament, for sure,” England captain Kane said in a post-interview area every bit as chaotic as the match.

“We spoke before the Nations League campaign that we want to use these games to really improve, really stamp our identity on how we want to move going forward.

“No better game than Spain away after they’re unbeaten in 40-odd games to show that, and what a performance. Up until the red card it was dominant, clinical, high intensity and they couldn’t live with it.

“It was a shame the red card happened because I think it could have been more and that’s been our mindset. That it doesn’t matter what the scoreline is – we go and we go and we go. You saw that out there tonight.

“In the end, we had to find a different way to win with the red card, obviously, and it was similar to a Mexico feeling where we’re digging deep.

“But when you can do both sides of the game like that it means you’re a very good team, so credit to everyone involved. It’s been a great campaign so far and we can end the year with our heads held high.”

Kane loved England’s dominance against “one of the best teams in recent history”, which only underlined his belief that nobody can live with them “when we make it at Premier League pace, intensity”.

The Ballon d’Or winner says the fact Spain could not handle that tempo should give them confidence in an approach that has developed during post-World Cup discussions.

The Argentina surrender has naturally been among the key topics and Kane told BBC Radio 5 Live: “We’ve spoke a lot since the World Cup about if we’re in a situation like that again, where maybe we’re 1-0 up what do we want to be?

“Do we want to be a team that sits back, or do we want to be a team that goes after two, goes after three? And that’s the team that we spoke about and it’s a perfect chance to show that and we did.

“It was really enjoyable to be a part of because it’s a feeling that maybe in an England team we haven’t had so much, especially against the top teams.”

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Hayes is enjoying success as boss of the US women’s team and Kyle Martino has suggested she should also take charge of the men’s side following Mauricio Pochettino’s departure

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Former international Kyle Martino has outlandishly called for Emma Hayes to be the new head coach of the USA men’s team and manage both the USMNT and the women’s side.

USA men are searching for a new coach after it was confirmed on Friday that current boss Mauricio Pochettino will take the Manchester United job later this week after a little over two years in the job.

Ex-Manchester City manager Pep Guardiola is reportedly a “top target” for US Soccer, while the likes of former Germany boss Julian Nagelsmann, Nashville SC coach B.J. Callaghan and current US under-23s boss Steve Cherundolo are also towards the top of the betting.

But Martino – who won eight caps for the USMNT between 2002 and 2006 while playing his club football for the likes of Columbus Crew and LA Galaxy – has thrown an unlikely name into the mix in the form of Hayes, who is the popular manager of the US women’s team (USWNT), led them to Olympic gold just two months into the job back in 2024 and is now preparing for the 2027 World Cup, where the US will look to reclaim the title they lost to Spain in 2023.

Martino was speaking on TNT Sports before the USA’s 6-0 win over Haiti in the first leg of the Concacaf Nations League quarter-final over the weekend and his suggestion drew puzzled looks from fellow pundits Brad Guzan and DaMarcus Beasley.

“I’ve got a name for you guys – and this isn't clickbait,” said the 45-year-old, before making a proposal that many would call the definition of clickbait. “This is a conversation starter, although I’m sure the trolls are going to come out from underneath their bridges and get their thumbs busy.

“Emma Hayes. Hear me out here! Emma Hayes is one of the best coaches in the world. She’s got an incredible résumé. She’s done it abroad and done it here. She’s got a great relationship with US Soccer and she’s got a great relationship with the fans.

“We have equal pay for our [men’s and women’s] players. We were a country that led the charge there, with other nations, let’s lead the charge on equal opportunities. Very rarely does it overlap. The women’s World Cup overlaps with the [men’s] Gold Cup [next summer] but I’ve got an answer there. Let [Steve] Cherundolo [men’s under-23 coach] take the Olympic team to the Gold Cup.

“Emma Hayes. Right now. It’s a commercial business at the end of the day. Let Emma do it. You’ve got a national training centre – both teams there at the same time. Let Emma do both!

“Manage both teams. Manage the men and women at the same time. No one’s ever done it, let’s do it. Let's lead the world of sports."

Hayes made her name during a trophy-laden 12 years at Chelsea, winning seven Women’s Super League titles and five FA Cups, before taking over as USWNT boss in 2024 and immediately securing gold at the Paris Olympics.

She had previously worked in the US early in her coaching career at the Long Island Lady Riders, college side Iona Gaels and Chicago Red Stars before heading back to the UK to be an assistant coach at Arsenal and then taking the top job at London rivals Chelsea.

And Martino – who ran unsuccessfully for the US Soccer presidency in 2018 – was adamant that the 50-year-old has the personality to manage the US men’s side and the opportunity is there for the federation to be trend-setters.

“She's one of the best coaches in the world,” he added. “I mean equal pay, we did that for players, equal opportunity, let's do that for coaches. Also she's just not only an incredible manager. She is one of the most entertaining people that I've have ever seen as well.

“It's a commercial business. She wins. And listen, if it’s complicated, then I'll say she only coaches one team. But I think her name should be in there.

“Unfortunately she's on the committee [to search for new USMNT coach]. Take her off the committee and think about her for the US men. Pochettino and her have a great relationship. So it’ll be a nice little transition, they have similar principles.”

Harry Kane last night became England’s record appearance-maker – days after signing a new Bayern Munich contract that’s reported to contain an intriguing clause.

Kane followed up his recent Ballon d’Or triumph by winning his 126th cap for his country against Croatia, surpassing Peter Shilton’s long-standing record, and last week he put pen to paper on a new deal keeping him in Germany until 2029.

That will take the striker up to the summer of his 36th birthday, although a key detail of the contract has given Spurs fans a glimmer of hope that he could still return to his former club before the end of his career.

As with his previous deal, it’s been reported that his new contract contains a clause that allows Spurs to match a bid from any other club for his services, should Kane leave Bayern before the summer of 2029.

Former Spurs and England star Chris Waddle doesn’t expect him to return to North London before the end of his career, though.

“People ask me ‘Do you think Harry Kane will go back when he’s 36?’, but why should he go back?” Waddle said.

“He might have a soft spot to go back, but do Tottenham want somebody back at 36 or 37? I don’t think so, even if it is Harry Kane. I think Tottenham are looking to move on and are looking at much younger profiles.

“The Bundesliga is slower than the Premier League, so at 36, he could still be wearing the Bayern Munich No.9 shirt.”

Waddle left Spurs himself to move abroad in 1989, enjoying a successful spell in France with Marseille, and sees how Kane has similarly benefited from playing in a new country.

“He made the right decision, and he probably never thought it would go as well as it has,” said the former winger, speaking in association with iGaming.com.

“When I went to Marseille, I didn’t know what was going to happen, and it turned out to be three unbelievable years in my career.

“I didn’t want to leave Tottenham, but when I look back, it was probably the best move I made. Harry Kane, for all his time with Tottenham – and he loves Tottenham, rightly so – would say that Bayern Munich made him a far better player.”

Portugal’s former captain hampered a golden generation for too long, but now there is nothing holding them back

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Even in the post-Cristiano Ronaldo era, the shadow of CR7 looms large over Portugal’s national team.

The squad for this month’s Nations League games was framed as ‘Portugal’s first since Ronaldo’s retirement’ by news outlets across the world. Manager Jorge Jesus faced repeated questions about the rift between the pair at last Friday’s press conference. Uncapped youngsters Rodrigo Mora and Gustavo Varela are already being compared to the legendary former captain.

That is to be expected following the international retirement of one of the greatest players of all time. But it also highlights how Portugal players and managers have been unable to break free from the shackles of the Ronaldo soap opera for two decades, often to the detriment of the national side.

Love him or loathe him, you cannot deny that Ronaldo’s numbers are staggering. In an international career that spanned almost a quarter of a century between his debut in August 2003 and his retirement last week, the forward scored 146 goals and won 234 caps, both of which are world records.

He captained Portugal to glory at Euro 2016 - the country’s only major title - and the 2019 and 2025 editions of the Nations League. There were also some brilliant individual performances, including a stunning hat-trick in a 3-3 draw with Spain at World Cup 2018.

At every tournament, Ronaldo dominated the narrative. Until Euro 2016, it was all about his quest for a first international trophy. The defining memory of the final against France was not Eder’s extra-time winner, but Ronaldo effectively appointing himself co-manager by joining head coach Fernando Santos in the technical area and issuing instructions, having earlier been forced off with an injury.

With European glory achieved, it was then all about whether Ronaldo or his great rival Lionel Messi would be the first to win a World Cup. In hindsight, Messi’s triumph at Qatar 2022 with Argentina was the worst thing that could have happened to Portugal.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

That should have been Ronaldo’s last international tournament. He scored just once and was dropped for the last-16 clash with Switzerland after reacting badly to being substituted in the final group match with South Korea, even though Portugal had already qualified. It was the first time since 2008 that Ronaldo had started on the bench at a major tournament.

In came 21-year-old striker Goncalo Ramos, who promptly scored a hat-trick in a 6-1 rout as Portugal produced their best display of the finals. Ronaldo came on as a second-half substitute in the quarter-final against Morocco, but could not prevent a 1-0 defeat.

An exciting new generation started to form in Qatar, with Diogo Costa, Nuno Mendes, Vitinha, Joao Felix, Rafael Leao and Ramos all in their early 20s. It looked like the perfect time for Ronaldo, then aged 37 and with his powers clearly waning, to bow out.

Perhaps he would have retired if Messi had not lifted the trophy, which gave the Argentinian a crucial victory over his rival in the tedious debate over who is the Greatest Of All Time. Instead, Ronaldo embarked on a selfish farewell tour.

Santos was replaced by Roberto Martinez and the new manager sought to appease Ronaldo rather than phase him out. Martinez took an array of attacking talent to Euro 2024 but Ronaldo was the only forward to start every game, despite failing to score a single goal.

The quarter-final against France, which Portugal lost on penalties after a 0-0 draw, highlighted how Ronaldo was now hindering rather than helping his team. The forward was ineffective but played all 120 minutes, while Diogo Jota and Ramos were left on the bench.

Two years on, Portugal arrived at this summer’s World Cup with arguably their strongest-ever squad, featuring back-to-back Champions League victors Mendes, Joao Neves and Vitinha, Premier League Player of the Season Bruno Fernandes and serial winners such as Joao Cancelo, Ruben Dias and Bernardo Silva.

However, Ronaldo again started every game, despite clearly being off the pace. The BBC Sport report from Portugal’s last-32 win over Croatia is telling.

“Their attackers always looked to get the ball to Ronaldo, even when better options were available,” the report says, adding that Portugal “improved” when the 41-year-old was substituted. In the last 16, Ronaldo was again ineffective in a 1-0 defeat by eventual champions Spain, but played 90 minutes.

That is three tournaments in which Ronaldo held Portugal back - three tournaments where a golden generation were forced to fall into line to satisfy their captain’s ego.

Of course, said ego ultimately led to Ronaldo’s international retirement. Offended by new manager Jesus' decision to leave him on the bench for September’s Nations League win in Norway, and then not to start him in the following game, he left the camp. Unsurprisingly, Portugal’s attackers flourished in his absence, with Felix and Ramos each scoring in three of the four matches in that international window.

While Ronaldo will continue to dominate the narrative around the Nations League games against Denmark tomorrow and Wales on Tuesday, Jesus and his players can now look forward to every camp without the constant balancing act of trying to keep their former skipper happy.

It means there is nothing preventing Portugal from being a leading contender at Euro 2028 and World Cup 2030. Neves, Mendes, Vitinha and Fernandes all placed in the top 30 of this year’s Ballon d’Or, with all but the latter aged 26 or under.

Several other players, including Costa, Felix, Leao, Ramos and Pedro Neto are in their mid-20s and already boast plenty of international experience. The older members of the squad, such as Dias, Cancelo, Silva and Fernandes, are all aged 32 or under and have at least one more tournament in them.

It is not the first time Portugal have had this powerful blend of youth, experience and star quality, but now they can harness it properly - free of the burden of having to “get the ball to Ronaldo”.

James Roberts is a freelance sports journalist working for FourFourTwo and other titles. He started his career at the Oxford Mail, where he covered Oxford United home and away, before becoming a sports sub-editor for various national newspapers.

#1043. Kane bends game to his will on record-breaking night

One day it will have to end for Harry Kane, but for now, almost 12 years into his England life, there is still no matching the wisdom and influence he has accumulated over all those games and all those goals for his country.

This would have been a great night by any measure for a man collecting his record-breaking 126th England cap. There was a handshake from Peter Shilton, now deposed as king of caps, and a flourish by Kane of his recently acquired Ballon d’Or, once his four children had accompanied him on to the pitch. These are the nights of which dreams are made, and yet – given the defining feature of Kane’s career – there was one more thing to accomplish.

That was a goal from the man who has ploughed relentlessly past the two great England individual landmarks of caps and goals. His second-half penalty won the game and, although he is not infallible from the spot, he is as close to that status as England have ever had. Age has not yet run him down, he can still bend the game to his will, and when it comes to the pressure moments, his longevity seems to offer the upper hand.

This was always going to be Kane’s night, with a great banner on the west side of the stadium paying tribute to the England captain. The Prince of Wales was in attendance for the occasion, too. Luka Modric presented his former Tottenham Hotspur team-mate with a keepsake from the Croatian football federation. Kane had to wait for the second half for the most valuable offering of all.

After the hour, the Danish referee Morten Krogh was advised by his VAR Bastian Dankert to take a second look at a corner tangle involving Jarell Quansah, and decided to award the second-half penalty from which Kane scored. It was certainly clumsy, but these grapples have been overlooked by referees in the past. The 27th successfully converted penalty of the Kane England era followed, and the man himself played the full game.

It just had to be him!! 🙌 Harry Kane gets his goal on his historic night, and England are back in front 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 https://t.co/7irrffchdH

Afterwards, Kane made a point of thanking the Football Association for organising it all, although it was also clear that this was no less than he expected. “It’s important to recognise the great players,” he said, “and it’s not something we have always done over the years.”

"It's a perfect opportunity now on Sunday to try and prove ourselves" 👊🏻 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 Harry Kane looks ahead to England's matchup against World Cup winners Spain, following tonight's 2-1 win against Croatia. https://t.co/m2OCkuN5kY

If the sentiment was a little awkwardly articulated, he is certainly right on the key point: so many England careers have ended abruptly at tournament elimination or elsewhere. Yet here was one being celebrated with the man himself, in what might even be argued to be his prime. Kane, 33, was asked again as to how long he might continue and did not rule out going on to 40, “if I’m performing at the highest level”.

That was a nod to Modric, a second-half substitute at the age of 41 and now on 207 caps for Croatia and almost 1,200 senior games. This Croatia team still seem unable to part company with their greatest player, despite his struggles against England in the seven-goal defeat in Rijeka. On this occasion, Croatia were much better.

It should have been more straightforward for England. They had taken the lead through Morgan Rogers midway through the first half and had dominated the first hour. But Quansah’s mistake gave Croatia an equaliser, and after Kane’s penalty England were fortunate to survive on occasions.

"It's a calamity of errors for England defensively!" 🇭🇷 Sučić equalises for Croatia https://t.co/GBxTSptUuF

“It was a tight match – a tough one,” Thomas Tuchel, the England manager, said. “We didn’t take our chances when we had chances, so it stayed a tight match. It cannot be glamorous and super-exciting [all the time]. It has to be serious and determined. We wanted a final on Sunday in Spain and we have that.”

The win means that England’s game in Madrid on Sunday against Spain, who beat the Czech Republic and lead the Nations League group by three points, has some bite to it. Another England win would mean they would overtake Spain on goal difference and win the group ahead of the Nations League quarter-finals in March.

This was one game when the players might have wondered if they were due more from a Wembley crowd that went through the motions in the first half and scarcely returned for the second. For the first hour, England dominated a Croatia side who often invited six blue shirts into their back line. Tuchel said his decision to select Dan Burn in the left-sided centre-half position over the left-footed Jarrad Branthwaite was almost split – a “51 per cent decision”.

England would break through just once, when Rogers got enough of his laces on an awkward Jude Bellingham cross deflected behind him and the shot brushed Josko Gvardiol on the way in.

The catastrophe of the defeat last month for Croatia meant they were naturally conservative. The equaliser was a Quansah error when the defender tried to head a loose corner back to Jordan Pickford and did not make the distance. Petar Sucic intervened and pushed it home with a right foot. England manager Thomas Tuchel, speaking to ITV: “Good win. We wanted this win desperately and I think we deserved it. I think it was hard work against a good opponent. It took us a while to grow into the game but after 15 minutes I think we did OK, got the goal and got better and more confident and had some good actions and good chances, good half-chances.

“Got a little bit sloppy at the very end of the first half, started the second half very good, didn’t score the second goal, conceded from a set piece, and then showed a good reaction.

“We got the job done and it was important because it was a special occasion for Harry [Kane] and he scored the winner, so perfect evening.”

On whether England were sloppy when they conceded: “It was maybe only three or four minutes before we gave passes away and especially in a moment when we were clearly the better team, we came with a very strong reaction after the half-time, had a beautiful chance created from Declan Rice and they blocked it on the line. It was like our third goal was coming and we had some easy ball losses in our own half that killed our momentum.

“An awkward moment in our box can always happen. It’s important to react and we did it.”

On his defenders: “Good. It was demanding for Dan Burn and also for Jarell [Quansah] because they [Croatia] play with a back five and have two number 10s in between the lines.

“It was a lot of work to do, a lot of communication but they did very well.”

On what will be better against Spain on Sunday: “I don’t know. Everything will be different. Completely different scenario, completely different setup, but I’m very positive that we will get what we want.”

England put in an the-Lord-Mayor’s-show performance following their 7-0 victory over Croatia. But it was still good enough to beat the same opponents 2-1 on the night Harry Kane celebrated his 126th record-breaking cap at Wembley.

Kane capped the night with the winning goal from the penalty spot, but a poor second-half showing – after Morgan Rogers had opened the scoring in the 24th minute – allowed Petar Sucic to equalise, aided by a dreadful mistake by Jarell Quansah.

To the exclusive club of Billy Wright, Sir Bobby Charlton, Bobby Moore and Peter Shilton, the name Harry Kane will be added on Thursday night. It is only the fifth time that a new men’s England international appearance record has been set in the post-war era, with Kane preparing for his 126th England match to surpass a landmark that has stood for 36 years.

“I’ll be the first to congratulate him because I think he’s done it the right way,” says Shilton, who will be back at Wembley to metaphorically pass on the baton.

“He’s not coming on as a substitute; he’s been out there every game, doing his job. Records are there to be beaten and I couldn’t think of anybody better than Harry, not just on the pitch but off the pitch. I am very proud of the record and handing it to Harry makes it not quite as bad.

“I think striker is the hardest position to play and goalkeeper is the second hardest because of the responsibility you’ve got. But scoring goals is the most difficult thing and Harry’s record in the modern game is there to be seen.”

Real Madrid winger Vinicius Junior has spoken about the reasons behind his underwhelming start to the season.

The Brazilian signed a new contract until 2032 in August, but so far his output on the pitch has ⁠fallen short of his own previous standards.

Press scrutiny in Spain has also intensified by the impressive start of Ivorian signing Yan Diomande, who has eclipsed Vinicius Jr in his preferred left-sided role.

Vinicius Jr said his reduced training schedule and summer transfer speculation may have affected his performances in the first part of the campaign.

“I don’t think I prepared as well as I could have after the World Cup, because the impact of that tournament is so significant for all Brazilians,” he told a press conference in Singapore on Monday.

“Being knocked out so early was something we ⁠hadn’t expected. So, I took advantage of my holidays to enjoy myself, rest, ​relax, ⁠and spend more time with ‌my family. I ended up training less than in previous years,” he said.

“That may have affected my start to the season.”

Vinicius Jr's future at Real Madrid was ‌a talking point in Spain for months as ‌he entered the final year of his contract before re-signing in August.

Premier League champions Arsenal were said to be interested at the time.

“On top of that, regarding my contract renewal, with so many clubs showing interest last summer, I felt truly overwhelmed, as with the situation at Real Madrid,” he said. “But it’s a very long season. “

The 26-year-old said he had a track record of hitting top form in the decisive moments of the season, and that he was on a positive trajectory.

“Maintaining such a high level for so long is always very difficult,” said Vinicius Jr. “I think only ‌Cristiano Ronaldo and (Lionel) Messi have managed to do this for so ​many years, reaching the same kinds of numbers.”

“I am human, I often make mistakes, but I always try to improve.”

Vinicius Jr has only scored one goal and recorded three ⁠assists in his 12 Real Madrid appearances this season.

Coach Jose Mourinho has only used him for a ‌full 90 minutes on ​three occasions.

Nevertheless, he did score twice on Saturday in Brazil's 3-2 loss to Japan, and is likely to feature in another friendly against Singapore on Tuesday.

The Djurgarden forward has hopes of jumping up four divisions if and when he eventually returns to England after his record summer transfer

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Nine months ago, an away trip for 23-year-old forward Abdul Abdulmalik meant going to Tamworth, Halifax Town or Solihull Moors.

Now, after a non-league record £1.5m move following an unlikely but much-publicised transfer saga, Abdulmalik is putting his wits against the likes of Malmo, Goteborg and Hammerby in the Swedish top flight.

And, if Djurgarden's final couple of games of the 2026 season go to plan over the next few weeks, Abdulmalik could well be playing continental football next season in the Conference League.

Its been a remarkable journey for Abdulmalik, who told FourFourTwo: "I knew that there was interest in me [in the summer], but I didn’t know how interested certain clubs were. There were teams in League One and in the Championship that were interested, but it doesn’t really mean much if they don’t then put any offers in.

"People were just making jokes. They were saying one team bid £85 million but Boreham Wood said no because they wanted £100m. They are all just silly in the end, but that’s social media and people just like to make jokes and have fun.

"To be honest once I knew there was interest from Djurgarden and I knew there was money being put in for me, I wanted to go. I told Boreham Wood I wanted to because it’s the type of opportunity that doesn’t come along everyday.

"I'd say there were two or three key factors as to why I wanted to come. Firstly the amount of interest from the sporting director Max Hahn and his keenness to get me here was massive.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

"Then it was the fact that we could win things as well – the opportunity to win the league and a European title.

"Going from playing in non-league to Europe is quite a big jump and I did feel like I was ready for it. Obviously I didn't know this at the time but the fans are so supportive too."

Abdulmalik's start in non-league has, inevitably, led to the familiar comparison to Jamie Vardy's route from Stocksbridge Park Steels to a Premier League title and England caps.

"If I even get close to what [Vardy] achieved in football I’ll be proud - but I feel like we have had very different pathways," Abdulmalik said.

"He was bought by Leicester at 25 years old from non-league [Fleetwood] and made the jump up to the Championship. I've gone to Sweden. I feel like we have had different routes. But, as I say, if I can achieve something even similar to what he did, I’d be very, very proud.

"Obviously there hasn’t been a player bought from non-league for this much before, but to have this opportunity to go and perform at this level is something I've always wanted to do.

"Physically playing men’s football in England, especially non-league, is not easy. In my first season, I wasn’t playing as much and I was getting quite frustrated.

"But once I got the opportunity to play, I proved why I should be in the team. I started to understand the game better. I felt like I was doing fine. I was then able to play my own game and show what I can do properly. It all helped me build resilience.

"I’d say non-league is a good platform for young players because you get an opportunity to show people what you can do on a football pitch. You never know who's watching. This time last year I did not think that I’d be in Sweden, but that is just how life goes sometimes.

"I’d probably say I’ve just got to play my own game and try to understand how my new manager wants me to play. But, at the same time, improve on my weaknesses. At the moment I’ve just got to earn their trust really.

"You’ve seen so many players go from non-league to the Premier League, but again I don't know anyone who has gone from non-league, out into Europe and then back into the Premier League. So I guess the aim is to be a groundbreaker like that."

Harry Kane is England's all-time appearance holder and scorer - and he's still got a few more to break

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Harry Kane now holds England's two big records: all-time scorer and all-time appearance-maker.

That puts him in an elite league of players in world football to hold both, including both Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo, with the England captain having 92 goals to his name in 126 caps.

But there are a few more records that the 33-year-old could be chasing before he hangs up his Three Lions shirt for good…

The big one for Kane is that he could become the first man or woman to score 100 goals for England.

The England skipper has even referenced this one, telling reporters “it's achievable” after hitting goal No.92 last night against Croatia in the Nations League – and he would become just the fourth male player in history to hit that target after Ronaldo, Messi and Ali Daei of Iran.

The next big one on the list, however, is most appearances as England captain.

Kane has played 126 times now, but 89 times as captain as of last night, two behind the leaders Bobby Moore and Billy Wright, who both skippered their country 91 times each.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

In two years' time, he will surely be looking to step out ahead as England's all-time scorer in European Championship history, as he's currently tied with Alan Shearer on seven goals.

And should Kane go to the World Cup in 2030 and his goalkeeper not, he will break Jordan Pickford's record of all-time appearances at the World Cup for England: he already has the goal record in the competition for his country but sits behind the Everton man with 18 appearances to Pickford's 19.

And then there's most goals in major international tournaments: Kane has 21 across the World Cup and Euros, trailing just Messi and Kylian Mbappe – and though the Frenchman has time on his side, you never know given his poor record at Euros in the past.

The hunt for more records continues this Sunday as England face Spain.

#1039. What Scotland need to secure Nations League promotion play-off spot

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Scotland’s victory over North Macedonia keeps their hopes alive of earning promotion

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Scotland’s hopes of winning promotion to the top tier of the Nations League are still alive but they will need to pull off a remarkable result when they take on Switzerland tonight.

Sebastien Pocognoli’s side were given a boost following their 2-1 victory over North Macedonia on Friday which ensured they have the chance to overtake Slovenia in the Group B1 table and finish inside the top two.

The top two spots in the group will automatically be promoted into the A League for the next edition of the competition though a third place finish will keep Scotland in the B League, the competition’s second tier.

Scotland’s fate is out of their hands so what do Pocognoli’s team need in order to secure promotion this evening?

The first and most crucial aspect of Scotland’s promotion charge is that they must collect three points when they travel to Switzerland tonight. The Scots head to Sitterstadion in St Gallen with a clear objective but the task will be difficult against a Swiss side who have already secured top spot in the group.

Switzerland top the table with an unassailable 13 points while Slovenia sit second on eight and Scotland are third on seven.

Earlier in the group stages, Scotland secured a goalless draw with Slovenia before losing a crucial tie 2-1 at Hampden Park back in early October. That means Slovenia have a superior head-to-head record against Scotland.

Because, although a draw against Switzerland would be enough to move level on eight points with Slovenia (should they also lose to North Macedonia), Slovenia’s superior record would win them promotion over Scotland.

All that means Scotland must win this evening and move to 10 points in the table to be in with a chance of getting promoted.

But history is stacked against them. Scotland have met Switzerland five times and have only triumphed once. That victory came in the first meeting between the two nations back in 1996 thanks to an Ally McCoist winner and the Swiss have won two and drawn two of the following four encounters.

Despite that record optimists may say the Scots are due a win and Switzerland may decide to rest key players with the group already won.

What else must happen if Scotland are to be promoted?

Well, Slovenia have to drop points against North Macedonia. Should Slovenia win their final group game they will finish on 11 points and Scotland will be unable to catch them regardless of the result against the Swiss.

That means a draw between Slovenia and North Macedonia or a North Macedonian victory opens up the route for Scotland to leap ahead of clinch a promotion place.

However, that permutation feels extremely unlikely as North Macedonia haven’t earned a single point from their five matches so far. They’ve been beaten twice by both Switzerland and Scotland and lost 2-0 to Slovenia in their previous contest. Not only have the North Macedonia’s not earned a point yet but they have only scored one goal - in their most recent defeat to the Scots - and that will not trouble a competent and determined Slovenia side.

Yet, should the unlikely scenario occur and North Macedonia take points away from Slovenia at the same time Scotland defeat Switzerland, the Scots will finish second in the group and will be promoted to the top tier of the Nations League

A second place finish would also have a knock-on effect for Euro 2028 as, despite being a co-host, the Tartan Army would be place in an easier qualifying group with a pot two seeding before the draw.
