#1037. Uefa hit by legal complaint over power of elite clubs

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The close relationship between Uefa president Aleksander Ceferin and EFC chair Nasser Al Khelaifi has come under scrutiny

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Uefa’s exclusive agreement with European Football Clubs (EFC), the all-powerful lobbying group, has been the subject of a legal complaint requesting investigation into potential breaches of European laws on competition monopoly and “abuse of dominance”.

The claim has been submitted to the European Commission by the Union of European Clubs (UEC), who represent a wider base of clubs who do not feel they have a voice. It comes as the EFC plans for a global expansion, having evolved into a body that arguably now sits beside Fifa and Uefa as a third major power in football, as the representation of the major clubs.

That has extended from Uefa’s memorandum of understanding with the EFC that the latter can be the sole club body they work with, with the details never made public but now expanded until 2033.

One argument from the UEC is that the agreement concentrates power and influence over European football in the hands of a select group of clubs - and, by extension, their owners. Such influence has already played a significant part in two major stories over the past few months. The EFC have been cast as potential king-makers in the Gianni Infantino crisis, given how the future of his Club World Cup may be dependent on Fifa’s own memorandum of understanding with the EFC amid their global expansion plans.

The entire topic of where money goes has become a major issue in Premier League debate about its rules, since there is a £300m revenue gap between the wealthiest clubs and the rest. It is argued that the influence of the EFC - formerly European Club Association [ECA] - has facilitated a situation where about 50 clubs have dominated four out of five Champions League places since 2000, ensuring constant access to game-changing prize money. One commissioned study shows that major English clubs have received €110m in Uefa prize money in a single season, which is half the entire revenue of rivals like Fulham, Crystal Palace and Everton.

Furthermore, Uefa’s Club Competitions Committee must review every change to the format, access and prize money and has 20 members - but 16 of those are nominated by the EFC.

The UEC argues this breaches Articles 101 and 102 of the EU Treaty on anti-competitive agreements and abuse of dominance, while also going against the Super League judgment.

In its 2023 Super League judgment, the EU Court of Justice found that Uefa holds a dominant position, "or even a monopoly", over international club competitions. It also held that Uefa’s control over access must follow transparent, objective and non-discriminatory rules.

The UEC argues that giving one association exclusive representation of clubs fails that test.

Uefa themselves signed a co-operation agreement with the European Commission on 9 November 2026 committed to protecting “inclusive stakeholder governance” within the European sports model.

The EFC would contend it has repeatedly expanded, but 736 members are seen as having “neither statutory voting rights nor representative voting Board members”

The complaint further asks for the EFC to publish the memorandum, order restrictive clauses removed and require Uefa to change such rules.

It comes out of long frustration from the UEC and their wider club base, who feel they have no voice in the system, let alone the capacity to rise on merit. One common view has been that there are too many glass ceilings - but also obstruction to even joining a group like theirs.

Four weeks before the UEC was launched in March 2023, the then ECA asked they not launch and instead work within their body. This was declined.

Uefa subsequently told the UEC that they would have to bring 100 clubs together to have sufficient scale for recognition. This has not happened either despite growing to 138 clubs across 25 national associations, amid constant questions – including in The Independent – about a lockstep relationship between Uefa president Aleksander Ceferin and EFC chair Nasser Al Khelaifi.

Uefa have not even indicated what criteria for recognition would be, despite formal requests from the UEC.

This has put a series of clubs off membership, since they would be more comfortable with formal acknowledgement. As many as 59 clubs have asked that their existing membership not be made public, because of political pressure.

One account has it that the Baltic countries were making progress in the establishment of a cross-border league that would bring the revenue to better compete at European level, only to be told that the EFC would help them with media rights and Uefa approval - but only if UEC member clubs left that organisation and joined the EFC.

The legal complaint was written by Prof Miguel Poiares Maduro, former Advocate General at the Court of Justice of the European Union.

“The Court of Justice was clear in the Super League and other sports cases,” said Prof Maduro in a press release. “Whoever controls access to European football must do so on transparent, objective and non-discriminatory terms.

“No association can be given the exclusive right to represent all clubs while giving most of them no real voice. Such an arrangement simply hands a select group of clubs control over the interests of all clubs, and, in our assessment, that control has helped to consolidate their dominance of European and national football competitions.”

“A system where a select group of elite clubs is given the power to decide who gets to compete in European competitions, and how the revenues are distributed, does not only harm competition in European and national football. It gradually erodes the model of open and balanced competition that Uefa itself claims to protect. If Uefa is truly committed to that model, it should welcome this complaint as a way to challenge the growing power of the elite clubs and better protect all football stakeholders.”

Manchester United players will be put through their paces when Mauricio Pochettino arrives at Old Trafford

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Kyle Walker has revealed that Dele Alli was the only Tottenham Hotspur player he ever saw complete Mauricio Pochettino’s gruelling ‘Gacon’ running test during their time together in north London.

Pochettino earned a reputation in the Premier League for turning Spurs into one of the division's fittest, highest-pressing sides following his arrival from Southampton in 2014.

Speaking on The Overlap, a show brought to you by Sky Bet, Walker detailed the specific drill used by the Argentine coach to push his squad to their physical limits, and why it left such a lasting impression on the dressing room.

“We had the famous thing called the Gacon [running test] – whoever played for Tottenham will know the Gacon,” Walker said. “It starts at 145 metres and you have 45-seconds to get there, you then walk up five metres [to another cone] and have to run back. It’s a continuous thing and there were 16 or 17 cones.

“The only person that I’ve ever seen complete it was Dele Alli – he was an animal at running.”

Alli’s stamina was central to Pochettino’s blueprint at White Hart Lane during the mid-to-late-2010s. As the energetic attacking midfielder behind Harry Kane, Alli regularly covered more distance than any other player, led Tottenham’s counter-press and helped the club mount consecutive Premier League title challenges in 2016 and 2017.

The volume of endurance work under Pochettino became the benchmark for players to make the grade at Spurs, says Walker. So much so that when the right-back completed his £50 million transfer to Manchester City in the summer of 2017, the contrasting training methods under Pep Guardiola initially left him questioning his decision.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

While Pochettino prioritised relentless off-the-ball running, Guardiola’s pre-season sessions revolved almost exclusively around possession drills, alongside relaxed training habits from some of Man City's senior stars.

“I remember getting off in the pre-season [at Manchester City] and you’ve got Kun Agüero who’s just balling around training – bad trainer, bad trainer but he turned it on in the game,” Walker explained.

“I got back to my hotel room after and speaking to my dad saying, ‘I think I’ve made a mistake here.’ I went from a [Mauricio] Pochettino team of running hard and we’re going to run all over you, dominating that area and also with a little bit of quality from certain players we’re going to win the game, to looking now and thinking we’re doing hardly any running in pre-season because Pep doesn’t like running – we did a little bit but it was mainly with the ball.”

Walker’s initial doubts quickly faded as Guardiola’s ball-dominant approach delivered several Premier League titles and a Champions League trophy during his spell at the Etihad Stadium.

However, with Pochettino set to make a return to English football at Manchester United, Walker’s recollection serves as a reminder of the intensity and demands the Argentine will expect of his new squad from day one.

Pochettino's first game in charge is expected to be Man United's visit to Anfield on November 22nd.

Manchester United have identified Nico Paz as the successor to Bruno Fernandes and the man to build their new team around.

That's according to a new report that puts the Red Devils in the midst of a bidding war for the Argentine superstar, with compatriot Mauricio Pochettino about to take the reins at Old Trafford.

Pochettino is stepping down from his role with the United States to become the eighth man to take the Manchester United job on a permanent basis since Sir Alex Ferguson retired in 2013 – and there could be a huge statement made in the market.

Bruno Fernandes has been arguably the greatest United buy of the post-Ferguson era, but after having the season of his life last term, the 32-year-old has shown his age this season, and FourFourTwo understands that for the first time, the Red Devils are starting to consider life beyond their talismanic captain.

While Pochettino is widely expected to build around the captain when he officially arrives through the door, Fichajes reports that United are one of a handful of European heavyweights vying to sign Como superstar Paz.

The outlet stars that the 22-year-old is seen as “a key figure to lead the team's rebuilding”, adding, “the club views him as a clear choice to replace Bruno Fernandes” – but it certainly won't be easy to lure him, with rivals able to offer more.

Premier League champions Arsenal are named among the suitors as they “see him as the ideal successor to Martin Odegaard”, with the 27-year-old Norwegian out of contract in 2028, while Chelsea are also mentioned in an ambitious plan to combine Paz with Morgan Rogers, Joao Pedro and Cole Palmer.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Paris Saint-Germain are named as the final giant in the quartet to “intensify contact” with Paz and Como in December, though two stumbling blocks remain for all four in their bid to secure the playmaker.

When the Northern Italian outfit purchased Paz from Real Madrid, Los Blancos inserted an €80 million buy-back clause – and while Arda Guler and Jude Bellingham are currently shining at the Bernabeu, they also have a 50 per cent sell-on clause for any future deal.

This could drive the price up for Paz – along with any potential bidding war – with Como keen on receiving a £100m fee for a player they believe to be a generational talent.

United's pitch to Paz will surely centre on something that none of the other suitors can offer, however, in making him the face of their new project.

While Pochettino could well draw on coaching a fellow Argentine and note his excellent work in the past with the likes of Dele Alli and Cole Palmer at No.10, United have the space to allow Paz to flourish – if he is willing to take the huge leap to a side who are nowhere near competing for the biggest trophies at this moment in time.

Balogun is worth €50m, according to Transfermarkt. United take on Liverpool when Premier League action resumes after the international break.

#1034. Jurgen Klopp rages at Gianni Infantino being ‘worse than Sepp Blatter’

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The Germany manager is upset at the way the sport has been governed by Infantino and compared him to his controversial predecessor Blatter

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Germany manager Jurgen Klopp has launched a stinging attack on the role of Gianni Infantino as Fifa president and called on him to resign.

A bemused Klopp has been left in despair at the way he interprets Infantino’s leadership of the sport: “I didn’t think things could get worse after Sepp Blatter, but someone has managed to do just that”.

Infantino’s position was at risk after a bold move to sell off the rights to the World Cup as part of a private investor plan, without the prior knowledge of the Fifa Council and national associations.

But Infantino has weathered the storm and now appears set to win a fourth term in the upcoming Fifa election, with Africa, Asia, Oceania and South America’s associations thought to be aligned with the current president.

Klopp would prefer to see a change at the head of the organisation though, suggesting Infantino compares unfavourably to his predecessor Blatter, who resigned in 2015 amid allegations of corruption.

In quotes reported by BBC Sport, Klopp said: “I’ve been following football for many years. There are people who are much more knowledgeable about this than I am. But I think most people now agree a change would make a lot of sense.

“I didn’t think things could get worse after Sepp Blatter, but someone has managed to do just that.”

Klopp added: “Regarding Gianni Infantino, surely the next person to come along can do a better job.”

The deadline for candidates to be submitted is November 18, with former Tottenham defender Ramon Vega having already announced his intention to be a rival to Infantino.

Kozo Tashima, the honorary president of the Japanese Football Association is also reportedly set to mount a challenge and the Guardian reported on Monday that French Football Federation president Philippe Diallo could yet be a surprise contender.

Former Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger was touted as a potential challenger but it is understood he told European football’s governing body UEFA that he would not stand.

Ex-Southampton and Manchester United midfielder Morgan Schneiderlin backs one player in particular to benefit from Mauricio Pochettino's coaching

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Former Manchester United and Southampton midfielder Morgan Schneiderlin believes Mason Mount has the right profile to flourish once Mauricio Pochettino takes charge at Old Trafford.

With Pochettino set to be confirmed as Michael Carrick’s successor following Thursday’s dismissal, Schneiderlin has backed the 27-year-old to become an important figure in the Argentine’s rebuild.

Man United have reportedly agreed a two-and-a-half-year contract with Pochettino, paying roughly £7 million in compensation to release him from his post with the United States national team.

Pochettino will inherit a side languishing 18th in the Premier League table, ahead of a trip to Anfield to face Liverpool on November 22nd.

Having played the best football of his career under Pochettino at St Mary’s, Schneiderlin is convinced Mount’s work rate and technical ability will quickly earn the new head coach’s trust.

"Mason Mount is definitely that type of player and profile that Mauricio Pochettino likes very much," Schneiderlin said, via Comeon.com.

"I think he will do great under him. He loves players who don't have big egos, who work hard, and have quality on the ball. They can really develop under him."

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Pochettino's arrival at Chelsea in the summer of 2023 coincided with Mount's switch to Manchester, as the England midfielder sought a new environment. However, injuries and managerial upheaval have stalled his progress at Old Trafford since. Restricted to a 25-minute substitute appearance in last Sunday’s chaotic 4-4 draw with Aston Villa, the midfielder will now be presented with a fresh opportunity to establish himself.

Schneiderlin also highlighted Youri Tielemans, who arrived at Old Trafford from Aston Villa in a £35 million summer move, as another midfielder capable of thriving under the Argentine, pointing to the balanced partnership he formed with Victor Wanyama under Pochettino on the south coast.

"Youri Tielemans is someone who also has legs and great quality on the ball and so he gives you different options, and of course, look at my partnership with Victor Wanyama," Schneiderlin added.

While Pochettino’s teams are synonymous with high-intensity pressing, Schneiderlin stressed that his former manager isn't just a coach who likes to fill the pitch with runners. At Southampton, Wanyama anchored the midfield while Schneiderlin pushed forward - a method Pochettino can replicate at Man United by pairing deeper ball-winners like Carlos Baleba alongside progressive passers such as Tielemans, Bruno Fernandes, or Kobbie Mainoo.

"Victor was more of a midfielder who sat a bit deeper and was very strong physically," Schneiderlin explained. "Pochettino doesn't just need players with huge engines who run, run, run. He knows how to adapt to the specific characteristics of his players."

With minimal time on the training pitch between arriving in Manchester next Wednesday and facing Liverpool four days later, Pochettino’s priority will be stabilising a porous side. If Schneiderlin’s assessment proves accurate, Mount’s energy and tactical flexibility could be key to dragging the club clear of the relegation zone.

#1032. Efficient catalyst-controlled C–H arylation of arenes

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

We’re sharing this article early to provide faster access to peer-reviewed, accepted research. It is citable and carries a permanent DOI. This version is subject to further edits and will be replaced automatically by the final Version of Record. All legal disclaimers apply.

Direct arylation of C–H bonds in arenes offers a streamlined alternative to widely used cross-coupling reactions.1 However, native substrates lack the preinstalled functional handles that ordinarily provide both reactivity and control over the site of reaction. Consequently, despite long-standing interest in directly engaging C–H bonds as reactive sites,2–4 the design of general catalysts that deliver high yields across diverse substrate classes while controlling site selectivity remains a challenge.5–12 Here we show that a microenvironment around a prototypical palladium dicarboxylate catalytic site can provide high selectivity for direct arylation of sterically exposed C–H sites, while high efficiency is achieved using an advanced palladium(II) precatalyst and tailored diaryliodonium reagents for selective aryl transfer. The applicability of this system spans from electron-rich to electron-deficient arenes, while electron-neutral benzene, which is often a challenge for C–H arylation, undergoes successive sterically controlled arylations, delivering functionalized polyaryl compounds. In addition to removing the necessity for pre-functionalized substrates, the mild conditions enable direct late-stage C–H arylation and the installation of aryl groups equipped with functionalities that are typically either reactive in traditional cross-coupling catalysis, such as triflates, iodides, and boronate esters, or sensitive to the basic conditions, such as N-hydroxysuccinimide esters. The results emphasize the distinct synthetic value of palladium-catalyzed direct C–H arylation reactions and showcase a catalyst platform that facilitates high yields and control over site-selectivity.

Nike will provide the official match balls for the Champions League, Europa League and Conference League - marking the first time all three tournaments will have the same supplier - as well as ⁠the Super Cup, Uefa Youth League and ​Uefa ⁠Futsal Champions League.

The deal was announced by UC3, the commercial joint venture between UEFA and European Football Clubs (EFC), which launched the tender process in March, and its agency Relevent Football Partners.

The Athletic reported that the deal is worth around $45m per year.

Nike Football vice president and general manager said: “We are excited and honoured to return to the Uefa Champions ‌League, one of football's biggest stages, after more ‌than two decades, and to bring Nike match balls across Uefa’s men's club competitions.

“Football is the ⁠world's game, and the ball is at the centre of it, the one thing every player, in every competition, has in common. This is a long-term commitment for Nike.

“We will listen to the athlete's voice, push the edges of innovation, honour the prestige and tradition of these competitions, and make sure the ball represents the instinct, creativity and joy football brings ‌to billions of fans.”

Analysts had said the deal would boost Nike's ​visibility but was unlikely to address the company's underlying challenges, ‌including slowing sales and a lag ⁠in product innovation that have stymied the sportswear giant in recent ⁠years.

“In terms of getting its groove back, high-visibility corporate partnerships are not the silver bullet,” ‌Zacks Investment Research analyst ​David Bartosiak had said.

“Whether you're reinventing ‌the wheel or reinventing the ball, ​you're still not bringing any sort of meaningful innovation.”

Manchester City face sanctions if their appeal against their Premier League charges fails

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Manchester City are expecting a verdict for their appeal by New Year.

The Citizens were charged by the Premier League earlier this year for over a hundred serious breaches of financial rules, with a potential points deduction hanging over them in the meantime.

The league is somewhat in limbo with Manchester City having appealed the decision and no one knowing what the punishment will be – but now, the eight-time winners of the Premier League have learned that their appeal will be heard next month.

City continue to protest their innocence in the wake of an independent commission finding them to have inflated sponsorships over nine years to get around Premier League laws.

It has been suggested that the club could be given a record points deduction that will result in their relegation, with their future hinging on an appeal.

Now, the Financial Times have revealed that the appeal is set for December.

A verdict is expected in 2027, with sanctions to be placed upon Enzo Maresca's side if they lose the appeal.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

While the rules of the Prem mean that the commission has full control to pass whatever sanctions they deem necessary, however, there could be further delays, with punishments subject to appeal, too.

These delays could well stretch beyond the end of the Premier League season.

Fans of the club have maintained a strong face, taking inflatable bananas to show that they will continue to follow City whatever their fate.

City face Fulham when Premier League action resumes after the international break.

Ex-Premier League boss Sam Allardyce is not known for couching his opinions and he has strong feelings about the fallout at Old Trafford

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Former Premier League manager Sam Allardyce believes Michael Carrick’s dismissal at Manchester United has all but ended his coaching career, while accusing the Old Trafford dressing room of 'shafting' their former boss.

Carrick was relieved of his duties on Thursday after a dismal opening to the 2026/27 campaign had left Man United sitting 18th in the table with just one win in 10 matches.

Speaking to Boyle Sports and Footy Accumulators’ No Tippy Tappy Football podcast, Allardyce suggested the 45-year-old has neither the financial need nor the appetite to step back into a dugout following consecutive difficult exits at Middlesbrough and Old Trafford.

“I don't think Michael Carrick will manage at all again – I think this will have finished him,” Allardyce said. “I think he'll be saying, 'I'm not bothered with any of this now.'

“It wasn't great, what happened at Middlesbrough, was it? And Michael Carrick, in his position, doesn't need another job in management, financially. He'd only need to do it if he wants to go out and prove people wrong if he gets the opportunity again. But he may well just choose to slip away quietly.”

While Man United’s hierarchy pulled the trigger to pave the way for Mauricio Pochettino’s appointment, Allardyce insists the board showed patience and instead has laid the blame at the feet of the squad.

“The Manchester United board gave him as long as they could. But the players have shafted him,” he added. “You can't play for that man as well as you did last season and then give up on him for whatever reason.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“I don't know what's caused the turnaround, but he'll have an idea why the squad is not as good as when he finished last season.”

Allardyce also identified what he believes were issues in Carrick’s midfield setup, arguing that playing summer signing Youri Tielemans alongside Kobbie Mainoo left the team far too easy to bypass in transition.

“Tielemans and Mainoo can't play together because they can't run,” Allardyce explained.

“They can run, but not quick enough. That brings criticism from all the punters. But I'll tell you why they don't do more: because they can't. They physically can't.”

Pochettino will inherit a fractured squad next week ahead of a trip to Anfield to face Liverpool in what will be his first game in charge.

Allardyce’s verdict highlights the scale of the overhaul awaiting the incoming Argentine, and ultimately the heavy toll the Old Trafford job may have taken on Carrick.

#1028. Why James Trafford must now be England’s No 1

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Trafford’s brilliant performance in England’s win over Spain means that he now deserves to supplant Jordan Pickford in England’s goalkeeping stakes

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

As auditions go, it could hardly have been better. James Trafford was given the opportunity to show that he genuinely belongs in the England No 1 conversation by facing the world champions in their own back yard and he excelled.

England outclassed Spain for an hour and then produced a backs-to-the-wall display for the final 30 minutes to cling on for a famous 3-2 triumph – their first ever away victory over a team ranked No 1 in the world and a first win over Spain in Madrid since 1987. In other words, historic, and the defining memory of the clash will be Trafford’s remarkable double save in injury time to preserve the narrow advantage.

The 24-year-old brilliantly repelled Fermin Lopez’s effort before recovering almost instantly to get across and somehow tip Aymeric Laporte’s rebound past the post. He was mobbed by teammates and while no England stop will ever have the same resonance of Gordon Banks’ almost mythical save from Pele at the 1970 World Cup, this immediately enters the tier just below.

He made six saves in total throughout the game – a number only bettered three times by England goalkeepers in the past 15 years according to WhoScored – and even in a first half where he had little shot-stopping to do, looked supremely comfortable on the ball and was accurate in his distribution. He was vital in beating the energetic Spanish press.

Leeds United paid a record £45m fee for a British goalkeeper to prise him away from Manchester City this summer and that is already looking like a snip. He has the highest save percentage in the Premier League this year (82.2 per cent according to FBRef ), while only the league’s top two sides, Arsenal and Brighton, have conceded fewer than the Whites’ eight goals. Trafford has been a key part of a Leeds defence that is suddenly one of the meanest around and has enabled Daniel Farke’s men to establish themselves in the top half of the table.

A penny for Enzo Maresca’s true thoughts. Given Gianluigi Donnarumma’s inconsistent form this season, there’s a strong argument that City jettisoned the wrong goalkeeper this summer and that the Englishman – who is not only better with the ball at his feet but also three years younger than the Italian – will prove to be the superior player. Perhaps he is already.

In his four previous England caps, starting with his debut against Uruguay at Wembley back in March, he looked at ease, only really leaving the question of whether he could perform under pressure against the very, very best in the world and his display in Madrid answered that emphatically. Tournament football is another level entirely but at this point, it would be foolish to bet against Trafford stepping up and delivering on that stage as he has done at every other.

Which is why it’s now time for him to be anointed as England’s No 1 as they build towards Euro 2028. This is not to disparage Jordan Pickford, who has performed remarkably for England and continues to be a top-level goalkeeper but the upside play at this point is Trafford. The Three Lions have consistently fallen agonisingly short of getting over the line in major tournaments and, to be clear, Pickford holds zero blame for that fact, but the pursuit of such an elusive goal requires brave decisions to improve the fine margins and officially elevating Trafford qualifies.

Thomas Tuchel has already begun the process by splitting starts equally between previously undisputed No 1 Pickford and pretender Trafford over the past two international breaks. It’s notable that the more inexperienced man has been given the two assignments against world champions Spain. He could have been in goal for the more routine clash with Croatia at Wembley on Thursday, with Pickford between the sticks in Madrid, but instead Tuchel rightly decided he would learn more by Trafford entering the Metropolitano cauldron – and his man emerged without even being singed.

The German was non-committal when asked post-match whether he now has a new first choice. “There’s no number one,” insisted Tuchel. “It’s a good double save [at the end]. That’s what we wanted. He had a brilliant match. It only works if you’re top from number one to 11.”

But the England boss will quietly be thrilled with the selection headache he now has and it does feel like a changing of the guard is slowly occurring. It may be harsh on Pickford, who has been generally underrated during his tenure as Three Lions No 1, but elite sport is a necessarily emotionless arena.

Pickford has been consistently outstanding since his international debut in a 0-0 draw against Germany at Wembley in 2017, with Opta stats claiming he has made only two errors leading to goals in 94 appearances, with 46 clean sheets and a 74 percent save ratio. He has made 33 appearances at major tournaments and been an integral part of England’s most sustained period of competitiveness (two world Cup semi-finals, two Euros finals) in their history.

Since the start of the 2024-25 season, only Arsenal's title-winning keeper David Raya (39) has more clean sheets in the league than Pickford (27) at Everton and even this year, he is in a creditable sixth spot with a 73.7 save percentage in the Premier League.

He has never made a glaring mistake that has cost England in a big game but, under the radar, he had a slightly rocky World Cup this summer. Martin Baturina’s shot slipped through his hands for Croatia’s first of two goals and in the last-32 win over DR Congo, the 32-year-old was beaten too easily at his near post by Brian Cipenga’s shot for their opening goal. He was fortunate not to be sent off against Ghana when he ill-advisedly came off his line and clattered Prince Adu outside of the box.

Television cameras also caught Pickford in an animated conversation with Tuchel after a botched clearance at one point, with the goalkeeper giving as good as he got before his manager ended the discussion by shouting “do as I told you!”

Throughout his England career, Pickford’s distribution has been decent, although sometimes patchy and Trafford presents a clear step up in that department. Purely in terms of physicality, the younger man’s 6ft 6in frame somewhat dwarfs the 6ft 1in Everton star. He has surpassed his rival in a number of ways.

Pickford should go down as one of England’s greatest goalkeepers – even if there is a somewhat surprising hesitance from many to bestow him with that honour – and he will deservedly clear 100 caps. But the time has come for James Trafford to be crowned as No 1. He’s earned it.

#1027. England stun world champions Spain in one of their greatest victories

Thomas Tuchel may not have planned it this way, but in one night he gave us all the rich history of the England team at once: some glorious attacking football, some self-sabotage defending, a red card, a late siege and a fight.

This was the beguiling story of Spain 2 England 3, an evening that began with the world champions parading the World Cup trophy and ended with 10 Englishmen defending a lead with their last breath. England beat the world champions in Madrid, and for more than 30 minutes including injury time they did so with 10 men, Dan Burn heading the last ball out as per the tradition of a defensive rearguard action.

This was the game that had it all: including a substitute, in Djed Spence, who had already picked up a yellow card on the bench before he came on. It was a coming-of-age performance in goal for James Trafford. So too for Ben White, the 2022 World Cup departee who scored the third and lunged with astonishing effect in the 84th minute to block a Nico Williams shot.

Trafford again! 👊🏻 An excellent double save from the Leeds United keeper 🙌 https://t.co/L27oQFQO1J

This was a performance good enough to win a World Cup final, never mind Nations League Group A3 – just a shame England neglected to get to that World Cup final in the summer. The fight in question was at half-time as the players came off and White and Fabián Ruiz first tangled and others dived in.

There was so much to admire. England began the night testing Spain’s first-phase passing to breaking point. They began the second half counter-attacking Spain for two goals from Ezri Konsa and White. Then after Elliot Anderson’s red card, this was a different England. With Trafford in inspired form, they held off the relentless Spain for long enough.

Harry Kane scored his 93rd England goal from the spot and was replaced before the end so that Myles Lewis-Skelly’s energy could give the midfield one more lease of life. By the end, the excitement meant that Kane was unable to take his seat on the bench, and he stood alongside Tuchel in the technical area, cajoling and advising.

England have beaten Spain on Spanish territory in recent times, but it was the nature of this performance, its many qualities when the moment required them, that made it so significant. This was the end of a 43-game unbeaten streak for the European and world champions, and it was ended by an England team in their best form in recent years.

Only three who started this game – Kane, Jude Bellingham and Declan Rice – started the final of Euro 2024, lost to Spain. Tuchel’s pool of talent is deeper than it was for his predecessor but there is also a greater maturity to the way they play. The England manager called it the greatest performance of almost two years in charge “given the circumstances… who we play, where we play” and as ever for England just slightly too late.

The defeat by Argentina in the semi-final in Atlanta just stings that little bit more when one considers the craft and resilience England showed on this night. They were under the hammer after Anderson threw an arm over the shoulder of Lamine Yamal and was dismissed before Mikel Oyarzabal converted the penalty that followed. “Thirty minutes against Spain in Spain feels like three hours,” Tuchel said, although Spain had a long way back after the blitzing they took at times in the first hour.

They all had their moments. Anthony Gordon had a strong first half. Morgan Rogers was central to the two goals England scored in the 10 minutes after the break. Anderson demonstrated that he is one of the best midfielders in the world in the hour before his red card. Spain were without Rodri and in his absence his Manchester City successor was in control.

Tuchel encouraged his players to mount a ferocious press against the best first-phase passing team in the world. Brave, but it worked beautifully and for an absorbing opening 10 minutes, Spain looked all at sea. Such was the pressure, the Spain goalkeeper Unai Simón abandoned the usual build-up strategy and launched his goal-kicks to the halfway line.

Even when Spain finally found their rhythm at the mid-point of the first half, England adapted. It took them a while to manage the discomfort of being denied the ball, and the familiar rapid incursions and switches of play. The counter-attacking switch from the early period pressing Spain in their own area yielded the penalty from which Kane scored the first.

It was only another Jarell Quansah error that got Spain back into the game. His mistake allowed Fermin López to play in Yamal for the run in which he was fouled by Anderson for the red card and the subsequent penalty.

Quansah is trying to do the hardest thing asked of a centre-half: play the ball out from the back. His red card in Mexico City and his mistake on Thursday against Croatia have not helped. Nevertheless, John Stones had a tricky start in an England shirt and developed into one of the team’s most important figures.

From another breakaway Yamal crossed for the substitute Williams to score Spain’s second. They would push again but England held on.

Thomas Tuchel praised England’s “statement win” that ended Spain’s 43-game unbeaten run and secured top spot ahead of the world champions in the Nations League.

Tuchel and Declan Rice revealed they had both believed England would end Spain’s long unbeaten streak, and their confidence proved well-founded.

“This was of course a statement victory,” Tuchel said. “I’m happy the players felt so confident. I felt it as well. I also had the same belief [that England would win]. I think we felt it from each other.

“The result followed the performance. I think it was on the highest level in terms of belief, team spirit, togetherness and it was on the highest level football-wise, in all aspects of the game.”

Tuchel described the nature of England’s win as “the Azteca reloaded” in reference to the World Cup victory over Mexico, but felt the win in Madrid was the best of his reign as head coach.

He said: “Yeah [it was the best performance of his reign so far], given the circumstances and the pressure and the quality and where we played and playing against the reigning world champions. They were unbeaten in 43 games. So putting a performance out there in Madrid, in this environment, that was a very complete performance and the best I’ve had so far.

“The last half an hour felt like Azteca reloaded, to be honest. Again, it was a beautiful week. The commitment to get better is on the highest level.

“I said it many times, I love these players and I love the mentality .We’re building something and that was the next step. It was an amazing atmosphere. I will bottle it up for sure and then unfortunately we have to wait until the quarter-final.”

"Without the red card, I think we had a clear win" 🗣️ Thomas Tuchel gives his verdict on England's performance against Spain that ended their 43-match unbeaten run https://t.co/rPef21Gtov

Asked what beating Spain can do for England’s belief, before the draw for the quarter-finals of the Nations League on Friday, Tuchel said: “You want confidence, not only through results, but confidence through performance and the result follows.

“That’s the ideal process and that’s what we got. We got it through the whole campaign of the Nations League, we trusted the process and improved our game and took steps forward match by match.

“We had a fantastic result and performance in Croatia followed up by a very good performance at home against Czechia. We then got our homework done against Croatia three days ago and that’s what we always wanted.

“We wanted to come back and compete on the highest level and see how far we can push our limits and how far we can push the opponent with the way we want to play and stay true to our identity. The team did excellent.”

England survived a Spanish fightback to round off their Nations League group-stage campaign in style with a 3-2 win over the world champions in Madrid.

Harry Kane, Ezri Konsa and Ben White scored for the visitors with James Trafford pulling off a series of saves to prevent the hosts drawing level.

Whisper it quietly, but England are all over Spain. Kane’s clinical penalty at the end of the first half has the visitors deservedly ahead, while the hosts haven’t managed a shot on target. There’s a scuffle as the players walk down the tunnel, with White and Fabian Ruiz clashing to spark a confrontation between both sets of players.

Ben White and Fabian Ruiz tangled on the touchline after the whistle for the end of the half. FLASHPOINT.

"There's a bit of a clash between the players" Tensions boil over as the two teams head down the tunnel for half-time. https://t.co/i7gqP1uTiU

Never in doubt. The wait and drama doesn’t affect Kane, who steps up and slams a clinical penalty into the bottom corner. Unai Simon dives the correct way, but he has no chance of saving it. England have been brilliant and deserve to be in front.

WHO ELSE?! 🙌 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 Harry Kane converts from the spot just before the break. https://t.co/TY3BjmfaFw

Anderson plays a piercing pass through to Kane, who races into the penalty area. The Ballon d’Or holder chops inside of Cubarsi and the defender hauls the striker to the ground. The referee shows no hesitation and points straight to the spot. Spain are furious as Anderson caught Cucurella on the ankle with his follow-through when he passed the ball which unleashed Kane. However, it’s checked and cleared by VAR. The penalty stands. Anderson simply made a pass, there was no intended malice in his contact with Cucurella. Kane will take the penalty and the noise inside the Metropolitano is deafening.

Penalty to England! The referee immediately points to the spot after Harry Kane is brought down 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 https://t.co/WIXQcJafki

Kane drops deep and clips a cross towards Bellingham. The Real Madrid star reaches it, but his looped header is comfortably caught by Unai Simon.

Gordon pinches the ball off Zubimendi and England fly forward on the counter. The Barcelona man feeds Rogers, who attempts to pick out Bellingham with a lofted pass. However, Spain intercept and Unai Simon gathers. Yamal leads an attack at the other end, smashing a powerful strike high and wide.

It is really difficult for any side to maintain the tempo and intensity and pressing that England showed in the opening minutes. Spain have the ability, of course, to ride it out but they are lucky England did not score at least once and probably, deservedly, twice during that period. It is a shame for Thomas Tuchel that his bold approach did not pay off then.

For the last ten minutes, England have been penned in their final third. Spain working them hard and Yamal the man to break lines - and get every decision going. As Bellingham seems to be saying they need to hold on to possession when they win it and not just give it straight back.

Rogers is the next England player to be penalised for a foul after he goes in for a 50/50 challenge with former Chelsea man Cucurella. Again, there’s nothing in the tackle and the referee blows the whistle in Spain’s favour as Cucurella rolls around on the floor. Rogers and Anderson both turn away in frustration at the decision.

Hall chases Yamal and brushes his back. There’s barely any contact and the referee awards a free kick to the hosts. Luckily for England, they defend the delivery well and Hall avoids a booking. Yamal is beginning to influence proceedings. England’s intensity has dropped ever so slightly after a fast start.

Looks like it’s going to be a free-kick to Spain any time an England player doesn’t politely move out of the way and allow Yamal to go through.

Spain are forced into an early change as Pubill is injured and can’t continue. Pedro Porro is on and will attempt to contain Gordon’s directness.

England continue to ramp up the pressure on Spain as Hall makes a brilliant run and dodges a couple of desperate challenges before digging out a cross for Rogers, who gets there first in a crowd of bodies, but his prod towards goal deflects out for a corner.

Yamal picks up possession and drives at Hall. The Barcelona winger nutmegs the full back and is then caught by the retreating Rice, who receives an early yellow card for the foul. Yamal then waves up his arms to the Spanish support gesturing for more noise and they respond.

Harry Kane has a new chant among the England fans. It’s an easy one to remember the words to. It goes “Harry Kane, the best in the world” in recognition of his Ballon d’Or. Simple but effective.

Another time that Unai Simon has been forced to concede possession with a long ball forward. This is evidently the cornerstone of Tuchel’s plan for tonight.

Marc Cucurella is being booed by some of the Spain fans when he touches the ball. I’m guessing it’s the Atletico Madrid fans inside the Metropolitano, who hold his Real Madrid allegiance against left-back.

The England travelling fans are loudly signing Thomas Tuchel’s name - it seems all really has been forgiven from the World Cup semi-final defeat to Argentina.

England go close again! They press aggressively and snatch possession off Zubimendi on the edge of Spain’s penalty area. The ball breaks to Kane, who flashes a powerful, low strike just wide of the far bottom corner. England have been electric so far. They deserve be ahead. Spain look rattled.

England nailing Spain in the first pressing phase. They have not let them out.

Spain go long from a goal-kick less than four minutes in. They don’t like the England press.

England fly forward again as Gordon slips a ball through to Rice, but Unai Simon rushes out to close down the angle and block the midfielder’s effort. England look hungry this evening.

England should have scored three times in the opening two minutes. Looks like Tuchel has sent the team out on the front foot. Spain are all over the place.

What a chance for England! The visitors win the first corner, and from the delivery, Bellingham escapes Cubarsi and meets the cross from close range. However, Unai Simon makes the save by blocking Bellingham’s prod at goal. A loose ball then breaks to Gordon, whose fired effort is blocked by Spain’s defence.

How did that NOT go in?! Unai Simon denies an early Jude Bellingham goal for England in the opening minutes ❌ https://t.co/cFhUXdrERM

We are under way in Madrid. Before kick-off, the whole ground held a minute’s silence for Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel and those affected by the high-speed train crash in Spain last month.

England go first. There are plenty of boos and whistle from the crowd. Spain’s is then belted out by a roaring stadium.

There was loud booing and whistling from the Spain fans as the England team was read over the loud speakers and shown on the screens inside the stadium. There’s still a lot of supporters who haven’t got in yet as there are empty seats in every section.

This is the first time Spain have played in their capital since winning the World Cup in July. Tonight’s captain Unai Simon is handed the trophy by 2010 World Cup winner Iker Casillas, before lifting it up in front of the adoring crowd. England have to stand there and watch. Will it serve as added motivation? Most definitely.

Spain’s goalkeeper Unai Simon doing what can only be described as ‘brandishing’ the World Cup in front of the England players to an adoring crowd. Duly noted by the England players.

In the absence of the injured Spain captain Rodri it is goalkeeper Unai Simon who has been presented with the World Cup trophy and lifted it high into the air to the cheers of the home fans.

According to my spies, only Declan Rice and Jude Bellingham clapped when Spain waved the World Cup in the faces of the England players.

"We will bring everything what we have to the table" 👊🏻 Thomas Tuchel speaks to Gabriel Clarke ahead of tonight's Nations League matchup against Spain 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿🇪🇸 https://t.co/FuzbmRyMX4

It is always interesting to watch Harry Kane go through his shooting drills in the pre-match warm-up. He’s just finished practising his shooting with Thomas Tuchel’s assistant Anthony Barry. He won’t be too worried, though - it would take a brave person not to back him if he gets a chance in front of goal after kick-off.

England’s back five is completely different from the one that started the World Cup semi-final against Argentina. The front six are exactly the same. It highlights the strengths of England and the problems faced by Thomas Tuchel who needs to find a more settled defence.

There will be a glimpse of what England could have had in the summer with Spain set to parade the World Cup before kick-off. Hopefully it will inspire Thomas Tuchel’s side. It feels this tie will help set the mood for the end of year appraisals as to how England have fared in 2026.

Thomas Tuchel will speak openly to England’s players about what they should do if they encounter racism in the Nations League Group 3 decider with Spain.

This is the first time England have faced Spain in Madrid since November 2004 when they were beaten 1-0 in the Santiago Bernabéu, a game that was ravaged by obscene chanting. The nations were supposed to play a fixture in the Spanish capital in 2008, but the Football Association insisted it be moved to Seville instead.

Earlier this year, Spanish supporters brought shame on themselves again after a flurry of anti-Muslim chants marred a friendly against Egypt; they were fined $20,000 by Fifa and must play their next friendly in a partially closed stadium.

There will be a full house in the Wanda Metropolitano on Sunday night, as the reigning world and European champions aim to defend their extraordinary unbeaten run of 43 games, and England head coach Tuchel is adamant the atmosphere will be in keeping with the occasion.

The German has, however, made it clear he and his staff will use their platform before the contest to remind England’s players of the steps they should take if the worst scenario unfolds.

Asked about incidents that had pockmarked this fixture before, Tuchel said: “I think I hear it the first time that this happens. I think it’s unacceptable. In any stadium, not even in stadiums, we will never accept racism. We will never be racist towards anyone.

Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of England’s final Nations League Group 3 decider as Thomas Tuchel’s side take on Spain at Metropolitano Stadium in Madrid.

Although both countries are safely through to the quarter-finals, England will seek revenge on Spain, who beat them in the Euro 2024 final and in their previous Nations League face-off on September 26 at Wembley. That day, Luis de la Fuente’s men profited from Harry Kane’s uncharacteristic penalty miss, England’s general wastefulness in front of goal and some seriously lacklustre defending to earn a chaotic 3-2 comeback victory after falling 2-1 behind at half-time.

Since that defeat, England have won four successive Nations League fixtures against the Czech Republic and Croatia by an aggregate score of 14-1. Last time out, they beat Croatia on Thursday, earning a 2-1 win as Kane, who became England’s most-capped men’s player with 126 appearances, dispatched a second-half penalty to seal the three points. Spearheaded by the Ballon d’Or holder’s brilliance, England must win this evening in order to overtake Spain and top the group.

🇪🇸 ALL SET FOR TONIGHT'S BIG SHOWDOWN! 🔥 The Spanish flag is flying high over the Metropolitano, ready to welcome both teams and all the fans for a night of football to remember. ❤️ #VamosEspaña | #NationsLeague https://t.co/EClJMbjxfj

Speaking ahead of the match, Tuchel said: “I think we are ready to win. Now it’s important that we play with the same mindset that we played at home, and attack them and try to make it a physical game, and try to impose our strength. I think that’s what we want to see. And then you can never predict the result in football, never. But it’s important that we show the mindset that you speak of and the spirit, and we will. I’m very confident about that.”

Meanwhile, fresh from lifting the World Cup in the summer, Spain have a 100% winning record in this season’s Nations League. They currently boast a staggering 43-match unbeaten run in all competitions, since losing a friendly to Colombia back in March 2024. England’s task is daunting, but not impossible.

#1025. Nathan Collins ruled out of Ireland’s crunch Nations League clash with Kosovo

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The Irish captain will miss the must-win contest due to injury

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Heimir Hallgrimsson has been dealt a blow with captain Nathan Collins ruled out of the Republic of Ireland’s must-win Nations League clash with Kosovo.

The centre-back has returned to Brentford and will be replaced by Jimmy Dunne in the squad for the Republic’s final meeting of Group B3, where a win would secure them second place and a promotion play-off berth.

Collins missed the last international window with a calf issue and felt discomfort in his knee late in Saturday’s 1-0 loss to group winners Austria.

“He went for a scan here and it was decided he would go back to Brentford, doing more testing on him,” Hallgrimsson explained.

“We will wait to see what their experts will say on it, but at least he is not in our squad for the game.”

The Republic boss agreed Collins’ absence will be a big miss, adding: “But we have shown now that our depth is much better and the knowledge of what we are doing is much better than it has been.”

Kosovo are in the driver’s seat, one point clear of Ireland, who are also hoping to propel themselves into pot two for the upcoming Euro 2028 draw with victory at the Aviva Stadium on Tuesday night.

They lost the reverse fixture in Pristina 1-0 but showed plenty of promise in Linz, despite the result, and Hallgrimsson is eager to replicate those efforts.

“We need to get the same mentality, the same characters on the pitch against Kosovo,” he said.

“It is going to be as tough a game as it was in Austria, so just transfer that same attitude and if we do that we will have a good by-product, which is a win.

“It is clear we need to win the game, a draw will do nothing for us and that is our mentality going into the game.”

Hallgrimsson has no other fresh injury concerns after James Abankwah got over a cramp issue.

The Icelandic boss was full of praise for Caoimhin Kelleher, who has been a standout throughout the campaign and made several critical stops on Saturday.

The Brentford goalkeeper is aware of the impact a win could have on qualifying for what would be a home European Championships in 2028 but insists the focus remains on the immediate future.

He said: “Yeah, it would obviously be hard to describe, it would be an amazing experience, to play in a major tournament at home would be special.

“But I don’t think we can think too far ahead into that. Obviously we’ve got to focus on tomorrow and trying to get a good result and we’ll look towards that then when it comes.

“But we all know the opportunity that’s there for us if we can perform, so it’ll be a great opportunity.”

#1022. How Andy Robertson defied the odds to become Scotland’s greatest captain

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

A humble Robertson insists he is not on the level of Sir Kenny Dalglish, despite drawing level with the legendary forward on 102 caps, but Jamie Braidwood outlines how the captain carved out a unique legacy through work-ethic and commitment

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

It was a burst from the left wing that would be seen time and time again. Andy Robertson’s first goal for Scotland came on just his fourth appearance for his country, at 20 years old and only a few months after completing a £2.85m move from Dundee United to Hull City. The wider importance of the goal was ultimately forgotten, a late consolation against England in a 3-1 defeat at Celtic Park. But for Robertson, with his wide-eyed excitement and the determination to carry his run forward, it was the moment that set the tone for what was to follow.

Twelve years later, Robertson has joined the great Sir Kenny Dalglish on 102 caps after featuring in Scotland’s 2-1 victory against North Macedonia at Hampden, and another appearance tonight against Switzerland will take him clear. Passing his hero and legend for both his childhood club, Celtic, and adopted one, Liverpool, will make the Tottenham defender Scotland men’s record appearance holder on 103. It is only in keeping with Robertson’s humility that he is the first to insist Dalglish remains Scotland’s greatest player; it is only in keeping with Dalglish’s typical wry humour that he reminds Robertson that his own tally of international appearances would be much higher had competitions like the Nations League been around in his day.

“It’s not really about me,” Robertson said ahead of taking the record. "It’s about him [Dalglish] in my opinion. For how long the record stood, for what he achieved in his career, for the person he is.”

Hampden celebrated Robertson, too. What is not up for debate is the scale of achievement and the remarkable nature of his journey. His story is well known yet will be retold many times this week: how a boy released by Celtic for being too small and who worked in the Hampden ticket office while playing part-time with Queen’s Park would become one of the world’s best left-backs and a Champions League and Premier League winner.

With Scotland, part of Robertson’s legacy is formed by qualifying for three major tournaments in five years, when the Tartan Army had not previously been on the big stage since 1998. Robertson was the leader on each campaign under Steve Clarke, from the penalties against Serbia to reach Euro 2020 to beating Spain and Norway to deservedly make Euro 2024. Then, in the delirium that was Scotland’s win over Denmark to qualify for the World Cup, it was Robertson who provided another moment of inspiration when he poignantly remembered his late friend Diogo Jota and the promise they had made to each other while watching the 2022 World Cup four years before.

Robertson has led his nation with dignity and class and if insists that Dalglish remains the King, the counter is to suggest that he stands, by some way, as Scotland’s greatest captain. He has worn the armband 80 times, with an 81st cap as skipper to come in St Gallen, putting him well clear of George Young, on 48, and Billie Bremner, on 39. Robertson took on the armband just four years after his senior debut, at the age of 24. Should he continue through to Euro 2028 and Scotland, as co-hosts, ensure their place, he may lead the Tartan Army at a fourth major tournament and mark a 10-year stint as captain. The history of the Scotland men’s national team is around 150 years old, yet he would hold another record.

Euro 2028 could be important in another respect. For although Scotland have enjoyed a golden period in terms of qualifying for major tournaments, they have underperformed in all of them and have yet to escape the group stage. The missing piece for this generation of players, which they could hold above those of the past, remains out of reach. For Robertson, he will not need reminding that Clarke’s considerable achievements as head coach come with the reality that Scotland failed to perform on the big stage, with the 1-0 win over Haiti in Boston in June their only victory in nine attempts at major tournaments. Now under a fourth head coach with Scotland, in Sebastien Pocognoli, there is still time to amend that, with a chance to still secure promotion to League A, should they beat the Swiss and receive a favour from North Macedonia.

It has not helped Robertson that during his time as Scotland captain two of the other home nations have been led by talismanic captains in Harry Kane and Gareth Bale, players who brought attacking inspiration and who could change a game in the flick of a switch. Robertson’s rise and formidable peak at Liverpool came when he was part of a machine, where the driving runs of the flying left-back fitted in with the movement of the front three and the organisation of the midfield. At Scotland, Robertson has provided plenty of assists and thrust, but, unlike his old team-mate Trent Alexander-Arnold, he is not the sort to orchestrate from full-back.

Robertson has, however, worked to squeeze everything he could possibly get from his career. Perhaps it was overcoming rejection that made him take nothing for granted, but Robertson has made history by turning the ordinary into extraordinary: by showing up camp after camp, for never letting his country down. There is the work-ethic, the commitment, the desire to push for every cap as if it is his last. There are the personal touches, too, forming a spirit and a togetherness that took a Scotland squad further than they had done in a generation. But above all, Robertson continued to play the game in the way he always vowed to: as if he was a fan who had just come down from the stands. And in his relentless pursuit, he has made a nation proud along the way.

#1021. Arsenal's wait for home WSL win goes on after Earps masterclass

Arsenal Women vs London City Lionesses. Barclays Women's Super League.

Report and free match highlights as Arsenal's wait for a home WSL win goes on after a 1-1 draw against London City Lionesses; the Gunners have now drawn all five games at the Emirates this season; Frida Maanum's early strike was immediately cancelled out by Izzy Goodwin

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Arsenal's wait for a home WSL win continues as they drew 1-1 against London City Lionesses on Sunday - their fifth draw in a row at the Emirates this season - with an inspired Mary Earps denying the Gunners victory.

While the result extends Arsenal's unbeaten home run to 24 league matches, it is becoming an increasing concern and a spectre on the shoulder that the Gunners have been unable to secure three points at the Emirates this year.

Giving her view to Sky Sports after the game, Renee Slegers - managing her 50th Arsenal game - said: "We spent more time than we normally do without the ball; partly the game plan and partly them asking questions of us on the pitch.

"We create big chances, could have done more with those. That's the frustrating part. This is the fifth [home game] and we couldn't give the fans the win. Unfortunately we couldn't do it for them."

It was two early goals that decided the fixture too. Frida Maanum scored for a second game in a row - having netted against Barcelona in the Champions League in midweek - slotting home from an Alessia Russo cross to put Arsenal ahead.

But a minute later, London City were level. Leah Williamson lost the run of the lively Izzy Goodwin, and the striker lashed into the roof of the net.

From then on, it was a goalkeeping masterclass from former England No 1 Earps especially that kept Arsenal from scoring another with her counterpart Misa Rodriguez also making her fair share of saves, albeit not as frequently.

The Gunners simply could not find a way past the inspired London City stopper as Lionesses boss Sarina Wiegman watched on from the stands.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

The pick of her string of world-class saves came when she tipped a Maanum shot onto the crossbar. It came shortly after substitute Delphine Cascarino had also rattled the woodwork at the other end.

The result does little to improve either side's WSL standings, and Arsenal's hopes of finishing in the Champions League places takes another hit. They are sixth on 14 points - already six behind London City in third.

"We were happy with the one point, we wanted and needed three today," Slegers added. "Every game is three points for Arsenal when we play for this club.

"At the moment, with our position in the table and how we need to stay connected and compete for the top three positions for the Champions League, this one was very important for us.

"With that being said, the season isn't over. It's still November and we have to look at what it looks like in May."

10: GOAL! A sweeping move is finished by Maanum after Russo's cutback to give Arsenal the lead.

11: GOAL! London City immediately equalise as Goodwin fires into the roof of the net.

22: SAVE! Earps makes a good stop to deny Lisa Baum, who cuts in from the right-hand side.

27: SAVE! Misa Rodriguez on hand this time to deny Alexia Putellas.

29: SAVE! Again from Earps! This time it's a flying effort to keep out another Baum shot.

68: CROSSBAR! Cascarino pings an effort off the top of the woodwork.

77: DOUBLE SAVE! Earps pulls off another brilliant double save, first to deny Smith then Maanum.

85: CROSSBAR! Earps fingertips a Maanum shot onto the crossbar.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Analysis from Sky Sports' Charlotte Marsh at the Emirates:

Before Sunday's game, Sky Sports asked whether Arsenal have lost their fear factor at the Emirates this season.

The answer surely has to be yes - although after the game, Slegers was adamant that the fear factor has not gone, despite being without a win.

Teams have come to the Emirates and sat in a low block that the Gunners have been unable to break down more than once.

London City were never going to do that. It's not in their DNA. They closer resemble the Barcelona team Arsenal faced on Thursday where, funnily enough, they drew 1-1.

But what they might not have been banking on was an ingenious performance from Earps. While Arsenal did not have to worry about defenders sitting back, they did face a goalkeeper putting in one of the performances of the season. How's your luck?

She made eight saves as Arsenal continued to pepper her goal - her most in the WSL since 2017 - and the second-most in the WSL this season after the goalkeeper that replaces her at Man Utd, Phallon Tullis-Joyce.

When asked how she found the game, Earps told Sky Sports: "Tiring. It's a big point away from home.

"Either team could have won it in terms of chances. Happy with the point - would have liked three. All the girls put their bodies on the line. I love defending. It was tough today and I thought we did a good job."

It was perhaps made all the sweeter for her that her former England boss Sarina Wiegman was watching on. It is well-documented how she departed the national team, but it certainly showed the Lionesses head coach what she was missing.

Earps has had to bide her time at London City, with Elene Lete continuing to be the No 1 until recently. The former England No 1 has now started in three games, and while she is yet to keep a clean sheet, she will have staked a huge claim to the permeant spot with her performance on Sunday.

"Mary is amazing," her boss Eder Maestre said after the game. "It's not just because of the talent she has, she delivers the commitment and the togetherness that she can bring to the team because of her experience. Watching her in that performance was a pleasure."

Arsenal boss Renee Slegers to Sky Sports:

"Two good teams going against each other. I think we started the game well, score a very good goal, but we let them come back into the game too easily.

"I must say the players left everything on the pitch. They were absolutely dedicated, playing with hunger and focus. There are things in our game we must do better. We want to be dominating the ball. Being more ruthless. It's very basic but that's what it's about."

On Maanum: "She was very big for us against Barcelona and good for us tonight again. You can always count on her with runs into the box. The finish was very good."

On 50th Arsenal game: "I'm proud to represent Arsenal. I want to do everything I can for Arsenal."

London City Lionesses boss Eder Maestre to Sky Sports:

"We are happy because this kind of environment is always difficult to cope with, but at the same time, we want to win every game so we cannot be [too happy] just because it's the first time we've drawn against Arsenal.

"Our targets are even bigger. We have the hop to have the performance. We improve quite well in the second half. We had the chances, and they did as well.

"They're one of the best teams in the world and playing knowing that they need the points to push for the Champions League positions. We already knew how close it was going to be."

The former Manchester United striker is not impressed with the club's recruitment over the past few years

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Former Manchester United striker Louis Saha has delivered a damning assessment of his old club’s trajectory, insisting the squad has failed to improve - and may have actually regressed - while questioning their reliance on inexperienced forwards.

Speaking candidly about the current state of affairs at Old Trafford, the two-time Premier League winner did not hold back when asked if Jason Wilcox and the INEOS recruitment model put in place was working.

"No, definitely not," Saha said. "It’s very clear, and you don’t need to know much about football. Even my partner can say that, and she doesn’t watch much football, but every time she hears me, she can look at the games and have a very simple take on it."

Michael Carrick was sacked as Manchester United manager on Thursday and will be replaced by USMNT boss Mauricio Pochettino.

But Saha says the problems run deeper than the manager and pointed to the void left by seasoned campaigners like Casemiro as a primary reason for United’s struggles, arguing that the current midfield lacks the necessary steel and know-how to control matches at the highest level.

"It’s obvious the team has not improved, if it hasn’t got worse, because, I’m saying, Casemiro was a guarantee," he explained to FootballPredictions.com. "He was someone who had this experience, that aggressiveness at the right moment. I think we do lack physical power."

Beyond the engine room, Saha expressed deep concern over United’s recruitment strategy in the final third. While acknowledging the immense expectations that come with wearing the Manchester United shirt, the Frenchman argued that tasking young, foreign players with leading the line is setting them up to fail.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

"With no disrespect to other teams, it’s a special club, with the Champions League," Saha added. "I don’t think a striker should be young at the top of this team. For me, it doesn’t make sense. It’s a lot of pressure, especially when you come from another country. You have too many of those who don’t have the experience to be the solution, and I think that’s a big mistake. It’s just a big mistake."

Reflecting on Sir Alex Ferguson’s era - where Saha competed alongside the likes of Wayne Rooney, Ruud van Nistelrooy, and Cristiano Ronaldo - the 48-year-old admitted he is baffled by the current lack of prolific firepower.

"I don’t like to refer to the past again, but before, it was maybe four or five strikers who used to score 20 goals a season, and now you have only one or two. I don’t understand."

Louis Saha was speaking to FootballPredictions.com

#1019. Romelu Lukaku retires from international football after 16-year Belgium career

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Romelu Lukaku finishes his international career with 94 goals in 135 caps

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Belgium’s all-time record goalscorer Romelu Lukaku has retired from international football at the age of 33.

The forward made the announcement on Monday, a day after being an unused substitute as Belgium beat Italy 4-1 in the Nations League.

Lukaku had been named in the Red Devils' squad for this month's Nations League fixtures, but missed last Thursday’s 2-1 win over Turkey with a hip injury and then failed to make it off the bench against Italy.

He scored 94 goals in 135 appearances for Belgium over a run that began with his debut in 2010.

The former Chelsea and Manchester United striker revealed his decision in a statement on his official Instagram page.

“Over these 16 years, I gave everything for the national team,” Lukaku said. “I experienced every emotion imaginable. I was lucky enough to play alongside extraordinary teammates, to whom I will always be grateful. I want to thank them all.

“I also want to thank all the coaches who pushed me to give my best and trusted me to help the team. It was a wonderful journey, and I cherished every moment.

“To the Belgian fans, thank you for all the support you have given our team. I am proud to have represented my country at four World Cups and three European Championships. I will never forget those moments.

“I am at peace with my decision to stop here. It was incredible. I enjoyed it immensely. I am grateful. Thank you.”

His final Belgium appearance came in a 4-1 defeat by France last month.

He leaves the international stage six goals short of a century, having struggled with a number of injuries in recent years.

The Fenerbahce attacker was still a central figure at this summer's World Cup, finding the net against New Zealand, Senegal and the United States.

Those goals made him Belgium's outright leading scorer at World Cups with eight, moving him past the previous record-holder, Marc Wilmots.

Across a lengthy international career, Lukaku helped Belgium finish third at the 2018 World Cup. He also reached back-to-back European Championship quarter-finals with his country in 2016 and 2021.
